Machine Learning Meets High-Energy Nuclear Physics: From Pattern Recognition to Physics-Integrated Discovery

Abstract

Machine learning (ML) in high-energy nuclear physics (HENP) is entering a new stage in which physical knowledge is incorporated more directly into data analysis, simulation, and physics inference. This mini-review focuses on developments that have matured in the past several years. Whereas earlier applications emphasized event classification, pattern recognition, and surrogate models for selected observables, recent work has moved toward physics-integrated workflows: calibrated Bayesian extraction of QCD matter properties, dense-matter equation-of-state inference from heavy-ion and neutron-star data, generative event modeling, neural unfolding of weak physical signals, differentiable inverse solvers, gauge-equivariant and diffusion-based lattice-field samplers, and neural reconstruction of model functions in holographic QCD. We survey recent applications of ML in heavy-ion collisions, neutron-star physics, lattice QFT, and holographic or continuum QCD. The emphasis is not on ML architectures alone, but on how they enter concrete physics workflows, how physical constraints such as symmetries, conservation laws, causality, thermodynamic stability, and topology are imposed, and how uncertainty quantification and validation determine whether an AI-assisted result can support a reliable physics conclusion.

Keywords:
QCD matter; machine learning; heavy-ion collisions; neutron stars; lattice QFT; holographic QCD; Bayesian inference; diffusion models

I Introduction

A central goal of high-energy nuclear physics (HENP) is to understand the properties and dynamics of strongly interacting QCD matter under extreme conditions. Ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions create a short-lived droplets of quark–gluon plasma (QGP) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] that allows the study of QCD collective dynamics and phase diagrams in the high-temperature and vanishing baryon chemical potential region [8, 9], whereas collisions at lower beam energies produce baryon-rich QCD matter and probe the phase diagram at larger baryon chemical potential [9, 10, 11]. Beyond collider experiments, neutron stars provide a complementary probe of cold dense matter. Measurements of neutron-star masses and radii from radio and X-ray observations, together with tidal-deformability constraints extracted from gravitational-wave signals, can be used to constrain the equation of state (EoS) of neutron-star matter [12, 13, 14]. From the theory side, lattice QCD supplies first-principles information at zero and small baryon chemical potential [15, 16, 17], while continuum and holographic approaches extend the discussion toward real-time transport, spectral functions, and finite-density phenomenology [18, 19]. Each area constrains a different region of the QCD phase diagram or a different aspect of real-time dynamics; together, they provide a more complete understanding of strongly interacting QCD matter. Across these areas, many central scientific tasks in HENP tasks involve both forward and inverse problems. The Machine Learning (ML) methods can assist both by accelerating forward calculations and enabling inference from high-dimensional observables, particularly when the quantities of interest are connected to measurements through computationally expensive models.

This mini-review should be read as an update to the earlier review[2] that introduced the broad landscape of ML applications in HENP, ranging from event classification and learned observables to surrogate modeling and early generative approaches. The timing of the present update is motivated not merely by the growth in publication volume, but by a qualitative change in how ML enters HENP. Since Ref [2], several previously separate directions have matured simultaneously from proof-of-principle studies into components of quantitative physics workflows: full-event generative modeling, calibrated Bayesian and simulation-based inference, differentiable inverse solvers, symmetry-preserviing lattice samplers, and detector-level or online deployment. This convergence provides a natural point at which to reassess standards of physical validation, model dependence, uncertainty propagation, and reproducibility. Rather than repeating the general motivation for ML in HENP, we therefore focus on developments that have become sufficiently integrated with iphysics workflows to affect quantitative inference.

The experimental ML literature is already broad and highly collaboration- and detector-specific. Accordingly, the present mini-review is weighted toward theory, simulation, and physics inference. Section IV presents selected detector-facing examples rather than an exhaustive account of the many ML tools used in tracking, clustering, particle identification, triggering, calibration, data-quality monitoring, background rejection, and unfolding. This scope is stated explicitly so that the selection of examples is not mistaken for a comprehensive survey of experimental practice.

In heavy-ion collisions (HIC), the forward problem maps fluctuating nuclear initial conditions and medium properties to final-state particle spectra and correlations through pre-equilibrium dynamics, relativistic viscous hydrodynamics or transport, particlization, hadronic rescattering, and, where necessary, detector response. The related inverse problem reverses this logic: because the microscopic evolution cannot be observed directly, the properties of the produced matter must be inferred by confronting model predictions with final-state measurements while consistently accounting for experimental and theoretical uncertainties [20, 21]. The inverse problem is therefore not a literal event-by-event reversal of a one-to-one map. The experimentally relevant map is many-to-one because of fluctuating initial conditions, quantum and thermal fluctuations, stochastic collision terms in effective transport descriptions, dissipative evolution, hadronization and decays, unobserved degrees of freedom, finite acceptance, and detector response. Many microscopic histories can consequently lead to statistically indistinguishable final states. Only in idealized limits with complete state information, such as nondissipative hydrodynamic evolution at the level of the equations, can formal reversibility be discussed. In realistic analyses, ML seeks a calibrated posterior over latent properties or an unfolding of ensemble-level information; it cannot uniquely reconstruct the microscopic history of an individual collision.

In neutron-star studies, the forward problem maps the nuclear EoS through the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff (TOV) equations to macroscopic mass–radius and tidal-deformability relations. X-ray pulse-profile and gravitational-wave models then connect these properties to observational data. The inverse problem is to constrain the unknown EoS function using astronomical measurements [12, 13], often supplemented by constraints from nuclear theory and experiments. Neutron-star inference is additionally data-limited in a way that differs qualitatively from collider analyses. Only a modest number of objects currently provide informative mass-radius, pulse-profile, tidal-deformability, or moment-of-inertia constraints, and the corresponding likelihoods are broad, heterogeneous, and model-dependent. Large simulated training sets do not create new independent observations; prior sensitivity, posterior calibration, and robustness to simulator mismatch therefore remain central.

Lattice field theory presents a related but distinct set of computational challenges. The forward calculation samples field configurations from the Euclidean path integral and uses them to evaluate correlation functions and other lattice observables. This sampling can be computationally expensive because of long autocorrelation times and topological freezing, while calculations at finite baryon chemical potential encounter the sign problem [22]. The corresponding inverse problem is to reconstruct real-time spectral information from finite and noisy Euclidean correlators, an intrinsically ill-posed task further complicated by statistical and systematic uncertainties.

Finally, in bottom-up holographic QCD, the forward problem maps a chosen bulk action, including its potentials and couplings, to thermodynamic and transport observables of the boundary theory. The inverse problem can be formulated either as the calibration of a parameterized bulk model towards experimental data or as the direct reconstruction of unknown bulk functions from available boundary-theory data [19]. Once constrained, the resulting model can be used to extrapolate into regions where direct calculations are unavailable.

Despite their different physical inputs and observables, these examples share a common computational structure: a forward map connects microscopic properties and model assumptions to observable quantities, while the inverse problem uses finite, incomplete, and often noisy or high-dimensional data to constrain both the physical properties and the viable theoretical descriptions. Statistically controlled inference generally requires repeated evaluations of the forward map across a large parameter or model space, which can make direct sampling prohibitively expensive and demands consistent propagation of all relevant uncertainties.

Within this common computational structure, the recent development of ML in HENP can be understood as a shift from isolated applications toward integration into complete physics workflows. Early studies often used ML as a direct map from observables to physical labels or parameters, or as a surrogate model that accelerated conventional Bayesian analyses. More recent work reflects a broader methodological scope, a closer incorporation of physical knowledge, and more stringent standards for validation and uncertainty quantification. These developments build on the progress summarized in several recent reviews [2, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27]. Here, we focus on methods that have matured in recent years and on the specific roles they play in physics analyses.

At the methodological level, ML can now contribute at several distinct stages. Representation-learning methods extract informative features from high-dimensional inputs such as particle-level collision events and lattice field configurations. Surrogate models replace expensive components of forward calculations, reducing the cost of repeated model evaluations in Bayesian analyses. Neural likelihood and posterior estimators enable simulation-based inference when an explicit likelihood is unavailable or prohibitively expensive. Generative models, meanwhile, can accelerate the production of collision events or field configurations. These methods address different parts of the forward and inverse problems and should therefore be evaluated according to their specific roles.

At the physical level, known structures can increasingly be incorporated directly into the ML procedure. Equivariant architectures can enforce selected symmetries by construction, while physics-informed objectives and differentiable solvers can incorporate evolution equations or penalize violations of conservation laws, causality, and thermodynamic stability.

In situations where ML do not by themselves guarantee physical consistency, the relevant constraints must still be tested over the full domain in which the model is applied. This leads to a broader standard of validation. For example, a classifier trained to distinguish simulated EoS labels is physically informative only if its predictions remain robust against changes in the dynamical model, experimental acceptance, centrality definition, and nuisance parameters. A generative model for heavy-ion events must reproduce not only single-particle spectra but also multi-particle correlations, event-plane correlations, rare fluctuations, and any relevant parameter dependence. An EoS inference framework must satisfy thermodynamic stability and causality while providing statistically calibrated uncertainties. A lattice-QFT sampler must reproduce the target distribution and controlled observables, with its autocorrelation times, sampling of topological sectors, and acceptance or reweighting corrections explicitly quantified. Reliable scientific applications therefore require known equations, symmetries, uncertainties, and validation tests to remain visible throughout the ML workflow.

These developments take different forms across the areas considered here. In heavy-ion physics, applications have expanded from event classification to calibrated parameter inference, generative event modeling, detector-level reconstruction, and the extraction of weak signals from complex backgrounds. In neutron-star physics, neural representations and differentiable inference pipelines permit more flexible reconstruction of the EoS, reducing reliance on a small number of predetermined parameters. In lattice QFT, generative methods have progressed from demonstrations in scalar field theories to gauge-equivariant samplers in gauge field theories with explicit tests of exactness, autocorrelation, and topology. In holographic QCD and related continuum approaches, ML is increasingly used to reconstruct bulk potentials and other model functions from boundary observables and to propagate uncertainties into subsequent predictions.

The content of this review is organized as follows. Section II discusses how ML is changing phenomenological workflows: from learned EoS-sensitive representations to Bayesian dense-matter inference, detector-level event characterization, and generative event models. Section III treats Bayesian inference as a cross-cutting methodology and discusses.. Section IV turns to experimental applications such as detector-level reconstruction, background subtraction. Section VI treats dense-matter inference as a functional inverse problem from neutron star observables, emphasizing posterior distributions rather than point estimates. Section VII focuses on inverse reconstruction from Euclidean data and the recent transition from proof-of-principle neural classifiers to physics-respecting generative samplers. Section V reviews ML-assisted holographic and effective descriptions, where neural inverse methods reconstruct bulk geometries, thermodynamic functions, quarkonium observables, and transport coefficients. Section VIII closes the technical survey with foundation models, agentic scientific workflow, quantum machine learning and benchmark infrastructre. In all cases, the goal is not to present ML as a black box, but to identify where physical constraints, uncertainty quantification, and validation must enter. The structure of this article can be summarized by Fig. 1.

II AI for HIC Phenomenology Studies

Relativistic heavy-ion collisions remain the most direct terrestrial probe of hot and dense baryon-rich QCD matter. From the viewpoint of ML, they are challenging because the physics of interest is not an isolated physical parameters but a set of latent quantities—initial-state energy deposition and fluctuations, the QCD EoS, the shear and bulk viscosities, jet-quenching parameters, details in fluid-particle matching (particlization) and in hadronic afterburners, and possible critical or anomalous-transport signals—encoded in high-dimensional final-state distributions. ML methods are now fused at three levels: to learn representations of the final-state information for posterior-inference of QCD matter properties or desired physics, to accelerate or calibrate the event-level simulations, and to reconstruct latent physical information with quantified uncertainty. The present section will focus on theory-side phenomenological developments recently; detector-facing experimental uses are discussed separately in Sec. IV.

II.1 Event representations and learned observables

The EoS-meter in Ref. [28] provided an early and useful exploration of incorporating modern deep learning into HIC physics studies. A convolutional network trained on final-state pion’s spectra was able to distinguish different QCD-transition scenarios in HIC simulations [28, 29, 30]. The important lesson was not that a classifier alone can determine the QCD phase diagram, but that high-dimensional spectra may retain information about the thermodynamic response of the medium after dynamical evolution. This observation motivated later studies of spinodal clumping, event-level transition recognition, and criticality-sensitive representations [31, 32, 33]. The more recent question is how such information can be incorporated into calibrated inference with uncertainties.

Phase transition learning has also been tested with lower energy heavy-ion data e.g., in Ref. [34], the unsupervised learning and a confusion scheme was used to classify liquid-like and gas-like patterns from final-state nuclear-reaction data, obtaining a limiting temperature consistent with the caloric-curve method. The density and beam-energy regime differ from relativistic QCD searches; yet the lesson is also that a learned classifier becomes useful after it is tied to a conventional physics observable and a closure test, as emphasized in the recent review [24].

The representation of heavy-ion collision events has since become more faithful to the underlying data structure. In the CBM-energy regime, PointNet-based approaches treat an event as an unordered point cloud of particles and have been used for centrality (impact-parameter) and EoS-related tasks [35, 36]. Point-cloud networks are natural for HIC because final-state particles form permutation-invariant sets rather than images (in terms of matrices) on a fixed grid. More recent work has used point-cloud networks to learn collective-flow patterns between small and large colliding systems [37] and transformer-based self-supervised learning to construct compact latent features for HIC events [38]. The methodological shift is from supervised classification of a few labels to representation learning that can support multiple downstream tasks and can be interrogated with tools such as saliency, SHAP values or comparisons with physics-engineered observables.

Physics-informed neural networks have been used in quasi-parton description to construct a four-dimensional QCD EoS [39] over thermodynamic variables from first principle lattice QCD evaluations. This line of work complements lattice QCD input, hydrodynamic calibration, and controlled effective models by building thermodynamic identities and physical constraints into neural parameterizations, before they are used in phenomenology.

II.2 Generative event models and fast simulation

Generative AI is rapidly becoming one of the most active areas of ML for heavy-ion physics studies, especially for simulation speed-up. Earlier surrogate models often predicted selected observables or hydrodynamic fields on average. Recent works aim to generate full event-level information. The goal is not merely to draw realistic event images, but to learn conditional probability distributions over colision output. DiffHIC introduced an end-to-end conditional diffusion model that maps initial entropy-density profiles and transport information to final charged-particle two dimensional spectra [40], where the integrated and differential flow observables, higher-order correlations and fluctuations are reproduced well. Differently, point-cloud diffusion models such as HEIDi instead generate events represented as particle cloud consisting of complete lists of final-state hadrons, including momenta and particle species, and therefore preserve the natural unordered-particle structure of collision outputs [41, 42]. This is a substantial step toward AI-assisted event generation for next-generation heavy-ion experiments.

Generative models are also being developed for more specialized heavy-ion tasks. Denoising diffusion has been tested for whole-event simulation in experimental environments [43]; diffusion and image-reconstruction methods have been used for heavy-ion background subtraction [44]; Flow-matching models have also been introduced for jet-induced hydrodynamic response, generating final-state hadron spectra from initial γ\gamma-jet information with large speedup relative to full CoLBT-hydro calculations [45]. Such methods are attractive because hard probes and medium response require many repeated simulations over jet energy, position, direction, and medium evolution. A fast conditional generator could make Bayesian jet-tomography analysis substantially more scalable.

Generative event models should be judged by physics validation rather than visual plausibility alone. Reproducing particle spectra is only a first test. A useful generator should also reproduce multiplicity fluctuations, species-dependent correlations, anisotropic-flow distributions, event-plane correlations, centrality and system-size trends, and rare-event tails. If the generator is used in Bayesian calibration, it must preserve parameter dependence and provide uncertainty estimates. If it is used for detector studies, it must be connected to reconstruction and acceptance effects. These requirements are more demanding than standard image-generation metrics, and they motivate domain-specific benchmarks for heavy-ion generative AI.

The foundation-model language has recently appeared in this context because a sufficiently general event generator could serve as a reusable representation of heavy-ion collision outputs. Such a model would not be a universal simulator of QCD matter by itself. Its value would come from being a fast, differentiable, and conditionable component that can be inserted into inference, detector optimization, and rare-signal searches. In this sense, heavy-ion generative modeling is moving from single-observable emulation toward a more ambitious event-distribution learning program.

II.3 Subtle signals identification from HICs

Another recent trend is the use of ML to isolate weak or entangled physical signals in HICs. Hard probes and rare signals pose a different challenge essentially: the physics signal is often small compared with background fluctuations. Deep Learning has been used to classify quenched jets and to test how robust such classification remains under underlying-event contamination and model variation [46, 47, 48, 49]. A related direction uses Bayesian and information-field methods to constrain the jet transport coefficient from multiple observables [50]. The target is a controlled inverse workflow that connects hard probes to medium properties with quantified uncertainty. These applications are important because jet-medium response contains differential information about the QGP transport properties, but the relevant structures are embedded in a evolving and fluctuating soft background.

Nuclear deformation and initial nucleon distributions affect final-state flow and transverse-momentum correlations, but the inverse map is complicated by hydrodynamic response and event-by-event fluctuations. Interpretable neural approaches have been used to connect deformation information to final-state observables [51], and Bayesian imaging has been applied to infer nucleon distributions in isobar collisions [52]. Recently, self-attention mechanisms from transformers have been applied to detect nucleon–nucleon correlations using final-state hadrons produced in heavy-ion collisions [53]. A transformer without positional embedding naturally respects the permutation symmetry of a particle cloud. Furthermore, the study of nucleon–nucleon short-range correlations demonstrates that averaging learned features over multiple events performs remarkably well for identifying subtle signals. These studies are examples of a broader strategy: use ML to construct or discover observables that are sensitive to specific initial-state structures while suppressing nuisance variations.

The chiral magnetic effect (CME) provides another instructive case. Traditional CME searches are limited by large backgrounds from flow, resonance decays, local charge conservation, and final-state interactions. A neural CME-meter was proposed earlier as a way to learn charge-separation information from simulated events [54]. More recent neural-unfolding work targets the inverse problem more directly: reconstruct the time-reversed or less-degraded CME signal from final-state information and quantify how interactions obscure the initial charge separation [55]. Fig. 3 shows the space-time degradation that such a network learns to invert. The significance of this development is methodological as well as phenomenological. ML is no longer used only to label events; it is used to define an unfolding map between an experimentally accessible distribution and a latent physical signal.

The common lesson from these examples is that heavy-ion ML should be tied to a physical hypothesis. A high validation accuracy is not enough. The trained model should identify which information is used, how it changes under alternative generators or detector conditions, and how the result is propagated into a physics uncertainty. The most useful applications will combine learned representations with posterior inference and posterior-predictive checks.

II.4 Symbolic regression and interpretable model discovery

Most ML applications in HENP are optimized for prediction: a model is trained to reproduce an observable, while the learned mapping remains difficult to express in the analytical language of physics. Symbolic regression (SR) provides a complementary approach by searching directly over mathematical expressions, learning both their functional form and numerical parameters from data. It therefore offers a route from data-driven prediction to interpretable relations and, potentially, to physics-informed model discovery [56, 57].

The challenge is that the space of candidate expressions is discrete and combinatorially large. Modern SR methods address this problem using evolutionary search, sparse regression, or neural generative models for expression trees [56]. For example, NeSymReS employs an encoder–decoder transformer that maps numerical data to a permutation-invariant latent representation and autoregressively generates candidate equation skeletons, whose numerical coefficients are subsequently optimized [58]. The methodological objective, however, is not merely to find a compact fit: a useful SR result should identify a functional structure that remains interpretable, generalizes beyond the data used for inference, and survives independent physical consistency tests.

Applications to real experimental data in HENP remain limited, although SR has already demonstrated the ability to recover known physical relations from complex or noisy datasets [59, 60, 61]. Open-source frameworks such as PySR have further lowered the practical barrier to symbolic model discovery [57]. A representative HENP application is the study of Makke and Chawla [62], which applies a pretrained NeSymReS model directly to measured transverse-momentum-dependent charged-hadron multiplicities from COMPASS SIDIS data and ALICE p​ppp collisions [63, 64, 65, 66]. Rather than assuming a specific functional form, the analysis searches for analytical expressions directly from the measured distributions. A frequently recovered structure is

f(u)∝11+c​un,u≡pT2,n=2,3,4,f(u)\propto\frac{1}{1+c\,u^{n}},\qquad u\equiv p_{T}^{2},\qquad n=2,3,4, (1)

with the best-performing form given by

f3​(u)=c01+c1​u3.f_{3}(u)=\frac{c_{0}}{1+c_{1}u^{3}}. (2)

Its structural similarity to the Tsallis distribution [67] illustrates how SR can recover compact relations without imposing the corresponding phenomenological ansatz a priori.

More importantly, this example highlights what is required before an SR result can be interpreted as physics rather than simply as an accurate fit. First, candidate expressions must satisfy basic physical requirements, such as dimensional consistency and the exclusion of mathematically allowed but physically implausible functional structures. Second, generalization provides a nontrivial test: an equation skeleton inferred from one subset of kinematic intervals can be refitted and tested in intervals that were not used during inference. In the above analysis, the same functional structure describes multiple unseen (x,Q2)(x,Q^{2}) intervals. As illustrated in Fig. 4, the SR-learned form f3​(u)=c0/(1+c1​u3)f_{3}(u)=c_{0}/(1+c_{1}u^{3}) reproduces the measured pT2p_{T}^{2} dependence across several kinematic intervals, including intervals that were not used to infer the equation skeleton. This cross-interval behavior provides a nontrivial test that the learned relation captures a common functional structure rather than a local statistical fluctuation.

A further validation comes from the extracted parameters, which exhibit consistency with an independent relation motivated by the Gaussian description of the average transverse momentum. Such a comparison is particularly important for SR: agreement with an independent physical relation provides a physics-level consistency check that is stronger than the numerical quality of the original fit alone. In this sense, cross-domain generalization and independent physical consistency provide complementary tests of whether a symbolic expression has captured useful physics.

These requirements also expose a central limitation of current SR approaches. Uncertainty quantification, failure-rate characterization, and systematic reporting of unsuccessful inferences remain underdeveloped, particularly for neural SR methods. A compact and interpretable expression is therefore not, by itself, evidence for a new physical law. At its present stage, SR is better viewed as a hypothesis-generation framework: it proposes candidate analytical structures that must subsequently be tested against symmetries, dimensions, known limits, independent observables, and uncertainty estimates. The longer-term opportunity for HENP is to combine symbolic search with such physics constraints, turning data-driven functional discovery into a systematic pipeline for interpretable and testable model discovery.

III Bayesian Inference

Given a model ℳ\mathcal{M} with parameters collectively denoted by 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, Bayesian inference determines their probability distribution conditioned on data 𝑫\boldsymbol{D}:

p⁡(𝜽∣𝑫,ℳ)=p⁡(𝑫∣𝜽,ℳ)​p​(𝜽∣ℳ)p⁡(𝑫∣ℳ).\displaystyle p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{D},\mathcal{M})=\frac{p(\boldsymbol{D}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathcal{M})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{M})}{p(\boldsymbol{D}\mid\mathcal{M})}. (3)

Here, p⁡(𝜽∣ℳ)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{M}) is the prior, which represents knowledge or assumptions about the parameters before comparison with the data. The likelihood p⁡(𝑫∣𝜽,ℳ)p(\boldsymbol{D}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathcal{M}) quantifies the probability of obtaining the observed data for a given parameter set, while the posterior p⁡(𝜽∣𝑫,ℳ)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{D},\mathcal{M}) incorporates the constraints supplied by the data. The denominator,

p⁡(𝑫∣ℳ)=∫d​𝜽​p​(𝑫∣𝜽,ℳ)​p​(𝜽∣ℳ),\displaystyle p(\boldsymbol{D}\mid\mathcal{M})=\int d\boldsymbol{\theta}\,p(\boldsymbol{D}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathcal{M})p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{M}), (4)

is the Bayesian evidence. It normalizes the posterior and quantifies the compatibility of the model with the data after averaging over the prior parameter space. We use boldface symbols for vectors and ordinary symbols for individual parameters, data points, or observables.

Bayesian inference is a statistical framework rather than an ML method by itself. In HENP applications, ML commonly enters by accelerating the forward calculation or by learning otherwise intractable likelihoods or posterior distributions.

For sufficiently simple problems, the likelihood can be derived explicitly. In many heavy-ion applications, however, it is approximated by a multivariate Gaussian,

log⁡p⁡(𝑫∣𝜽)\displaystyle\log p(\boldsymbol{D}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}) =−12​[𝒚⁡(𝜽)−𝑫]T​𝚺−1​[𝒚⁡(𝜽)−𝑫]\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\boldsymbol{y}(\boldsymbol{\theta})-\boldsymbol{D}\right]^{T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\left[\boldsymbol{y}(\boldsymbol{\theta})-\boldsymbol{D}\right]
−12logdet𝚺−N2log(2π),\displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{2}\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi), (5)

where 𝒚⁡(𝜽)\boldsymbol{y}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is a vector of NN model observables and 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} is their total covariance matrix. Depending on the analysis, 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} may include experimental statistical and systematic uncertainties, finite-simulation statistics, emulator uncertainty, and estimates of model discrepancy. The Gaussian form is an assumption and should be tested whenever non-Gaussian uncertainties or low-statistics observables are important.

Heavy-ion observables are commonly estimated by averaging over many fluctuating collision events. Obtaining sufficient statistics at every point in a high-dimensional parameter space can therefore require a prohibitive number of model calculations. This difficulty is often addressed using a surrogate model, such as a Gaussian-process (GP) emulator.

The full physical model is first evaluated at MM representative design points, {𝜽i,yi=y(𝜽i)},i=1,2,⋯M\left\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},y_{i}=y(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})\right\},i=1,2,\cdots M, chosen to cover the parameter region of interest. For a scalar observable with its mean removed, a GP treats y⁡(𝜽)y(\boldsymbol{\theta}) as a random function characterized by a covariance kernel k⁡(𝜽,𝜽′)k(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}). The predictive mean and variance at a new point 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} are

μ⁡(𝜽)\displaystyle\mu(\boldsymbol{\theta}) =𝒌⁡(𝜽,𝜽i)​[𝒌⁡(𝜽i,𝜽j)]−1​𝒚​(𝜽j),\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{k}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})[\boldsymbol{k}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{j})]^{-1}\boldsymbol{y}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{j}), (6)
σ2​(𝜽)\displaystyle\sigma^{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) =k⁡(𝜽,𝜽)−𝒌⁡(𝜽,𝜽i)​[𝒌⁡(𝜽i,𝜽j)]−1​𝒌​(𝜽j,𝜽)\displaystyle=k(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta})-\boldsymbol{k}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})[\boldsymbol{k}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{j})]^{-1}\boldsymbol{k}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{j},\boldsymbol{\theta}) (7)

A commonly used choice is the squared-exponential kernel,

k(𝒙,𝒙′)=σf2exp[−12∑a(xa−xa′)2ℓa2],\displaystyle k(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime})=\sigma_{f}^{2}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a}\frac{(x_{a}-x^{\prime}_{a})^{2}}{\ell_{a}^{2}}\right], (8)

where σf\sigma_{f} controls the overall variation of the function and ℓa\ell_{a} is the correlation length along parameter direction aa [68, 21, 69]. Matérn and composite kernels can be used when different assumptions about smoothness or noise are appropriate. The kernel hyperparameters are usually determined by maximizing the GP marginal likelihood or by sampling their posterior distribution. Regardless of the kernel choice, the emulator must be validated against model calculations that were not used for training.

When many correlated observables are included, the emulation can be stabilized using principal-component analysis (PCA). Separate emulators are then trained for the retained few major principal components. The observables are approximately reconstructed from the inverse transformation.

The combination of PCA, GP emulation, and Markov-chain Monte Carlo sampling was introduced into heavy-ion phenomenology in Refs. [21, 69] and has enabled systematic analyses of initial-state parameters and QGP transport coefficients in high-dimensional parameter spaces [70, 71].

More recent work has explored deep neural networks as scalable and accurate surrogates for expensive forward calculations [72]. Normalizing flows play a different role: as conditional density estimators, they can learn likelihoods or posterior distributions directly from simulated data and thereby enable simulation-based or likelihood-free inference when an explicit likelihood is unavailable [73, 74, 75]. Posterior sampling can also be accelerated using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) when gradients are available [76, 52], while nested sampling provides both posterior samples and an estimate of the Bayesian evidence [77, 78]. These methods address different computational bottlenecks and should be compared through closure tests, posterior calibration, and computational cost rather than through sampling speed alone.

III.1 Bayesian extraction of the dense nuclear-matter EoS

A representative recent development is the Bayesian extraction of the dense nuclear-matter EoS from heavy-ion data [79]. In that work, a flexible density-dependent mean field was embedded into a transport-model analysis and constrained by proton mean transverse kinetic energies and elliptic flows in the beam-energy range relevant for baryon-rich matter. This marks a conceptual shift from pattern recognition to quantitative inference: the output is a posterior distribution over EoS functions rather than a class label. Fig. 5 gives the Bayesian inference of the high-density nuclear EoS from heavy-ion data [79]. It also highlights why ML and Bayesian methods are inseparable in modern heavy-ion phenomenology. Emulators and sampling strategies are needed because direct exploration of the model space is too costly, but the scientific result must still be a physics posterior conditioned on data and modeling assumptions.

Bayesian constraints on nuclear matter inputs are also being developed outside collider-energy observables. Recently, the BUU transport calculation of the iso-vector giant dipole resonance was used to infer the iso-vector effective mass and the neutron-proton effective mass splitting from the energy-weighted sum rule and width [80]. This is a low energy nuclear structure example, but it belongs to the same statistical program: uncertain effective interactions are propagated through a forward model and constrained by measured response function.

This direction is particularly relevant for connecting heavy-ion collisions to neutron-star physics. Heavy-ion observables probe hot, dynamical, and often non-equilibrium matter, while neutron stars probe cold beta-equilibrated neutron-rich matter. The two systems do not follow the same thermodynamic trajectory, but they constrain overlapping regions of the dense-QCD theory space. A useful near-term goal is therefore not to force a single EoS reconstruction from all data, but to construct hierarchical analyses in which heavy-ion data, chiral effective theory, neutron-star observations, perturbative QCD calculations, and lattice constraints each enter with their own nuisance parameters and validity ranges. ML contributes by accelerating the forward maps and by representing functional uncertainty in a way that can be propagated across sectors.

III.2 Transport properties of baryon-rich QCD matter

Early extraction of the QGP transprot properties focused on LHC and top RHIC energeis, where EoS and transport coefficients were primarily parameterized as function of temperature. Lowering the collision energy increases nuclear stopping and allows heavy-ion experiments to probe QCD matter at appreciable net-baryon density. The relevant transport properties therefore are the specific shear and bulk viscosities to entropy ratio, η⁡(T,μB)/s\eta(T,\mu_{B})/s and ζ⁡(T,μB)/s\zeta(T,\mu_{B})/s, and the baryon diffusion coefficient κB​(T,μB)\kappa_{B}(T,\mu_{B}), all as functions of both temperature TT and baryon chemical potential μB\mu_{B}. Their extraction is more difficult than at top RHIC and LHC energies because they are correlated with nuclear stopping, the longitudinal distributions of energy and baryon density, the finite-density equation of state. Consequently, realistic analyses require (3+1)(3+1)-dimensional models and observables over a broad rapidity range. And a challenge is to distinguish genuine finite-density transport effects from changes in nuclear stopping, longitudinal initial conditions, the equation of state, and the hadronic phase.

Earlier Bayesian study in this direct Auvinen et al. analyzed Au–Au collisions at sNN=19.6\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=19.6, 39, and 62.4 GeV using a transport–hydrodynamics hybrid model [81] and an effective viscosity as a function of beam energy is extracted. Since then, a major extension was achieved [82], using an event-by-event (3+1)(3+1)D dynamical initialization model coupled to MUSIC hydrodynamics and UrQMD hadronic transport. The calculation employed a finite-density lattice-QCD-based equation of state. The analysis included data of particle yields, mean transverse momenta, anisotropic flow, and pseudorapidity-dependent observables in Au–Au collisions at sNN=7.7\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=7.7, 19.6, and 200 GeV. The parameter space included nuclear-stopping parameters, the values of the specific viscosity at μB=0\mu_{B}=0, 0.20.2, and 0.40.4 GeV, and parameters controlling the magnitude and temperature dependence of the bulk viscosity. The analysis constrained the average initial-state rapidity loss and favored an increase of the specific shear with μB\mu_{B} up to approximately 0.40.4 GeV, and a preference for a larger bulk-viscosity peak at sNN=19.6\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=19.6 GeV than at 7.7 or 200 GeV.

A full posterior analysis of the finite-baryon region was further examined in Ref. [83]. In addition to standard GP emulation, the authors used a heteroscedastic principal-component stochastic-kriging emulator that accounts for the varying statistical uncertainty of different observables. Training points sampled from preliminary high-probability posterior regions were added to the original Latin-hypercube design, improving the emulator specifically where the final inference placed substantial probability.Posterior sampling employed a preconditioned Monte Carlo algorithm in which a normalizing flow decorrelated the parameters before sequential Monte Carlo sampling. The analysis again obtained strong constraints on nuclear stopping and favored an increasing shear viscosity over the range μB≲0.2\mu_{B}\lesssim 0.2 GeV. Full simulations at 100 posterior samples were then used to validate the emulator-based inference and propagate parameter uncertainty to pTp_{T}-differential predictions.

The emulator dependence of the analysis was further explored in dedicated closure tests in Ref. [84]. Different GP implementations produced substantially different posterior widths even when their conventional prediction errors appeared reasonable. Emulators designed to include the heterogeneous Monte Carlo uncertainty recovered the planted parameter values more accurately than a standard GP implementation. Adding training points in the high-posterior-probability region reduced the information loss by roughly two orders of magnitude in their closure metric. This study demonstrates that the transport-coefficient posterior can be biased or artificially broadened by the surrogate model itself, making emulator-level closure tests essential.

Nevertheless, the extracted viscosities remain sensitive to the assumed dynamical framework. Götz, Karpenko, and Elfner performed an independent Bayesian analysis using SMASH-generated initial conditions, vHLLE hydrodynamics, and a SMASH hadronic afterburner [85]. Their posterior favored a small shear viscosity in the high-temperature QGP phase and a moderate-to-large value near particlization. However, the μB\mu_{B} dependence of both the shear and bulk viscosities remained weakly constrained. These results emphasize that a narrow posterior obtained within a particular model does not by itself constitute a model-independent determination. A more systematic treatment of uncertainties associated with different dynamical frameworks will therefore be essential in future analyses.

Finally, a preliminary Bayesian determination of baryon diffusion coefficient was reported by Sarkar, Panday, and Chatterjee using STAR data at sNN=19.6\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=19.6 GeV [86]. PCA and GP regression were used to emulate the hydrodynamic calculation, followed by MCMC sampling of the initial-condition and diffusion parameters. The application of Bayesian analysis to the extraction of baryon diffusion is promising but was presented in a short conference proceeding and was based on one collision energy and two centrality classes. A more definitive extraction will require simultaneous variation of the initial baryon deposition, stopping, viscosity, equation of state, and hadronic transport, together with closure tests and a broader set of rapidity-dependent observables.

III.3 Bayesian jet tomography and ML-assisted jet analysis

Jets originate from hard scatterings during the early stage of a nuclear collision and subsequently evolve while traversing the QGP. Their energy loss, transverse-momentum broadening, modified shower structure, and induced medium response therefore carry information about the microscopic interactions between energetic partons and the medium. Bayesian inference has been used to constrain parametrized energy-loss distributions and transport coefficients, while ML tools have been introduced to accelerate the required simulations, reconstruct jet properties, and identify informative observables.

An early data-driven extraction of jet energy loss was performed using inclusive and photon-triggered jet spectra in Pb–Pb collisions [87]. The energy-loss distribution was characterized by its average and fluctuations, both inferred from experimental data. The extracted distributions were found to be consistent with Linear Boltzmann Transport calculations, demonstrating how Bayesian inference can connect effective energy-loss descriptions with microscopic transport simulations. Following this approach, the average energy loss of full jets was extracted from inclusive jet spectra for different collision systems and centralities [88]. The suppression of J/ψJ/\psi production was also shown to provide sensitivity to the energy loss of gluon-initiated jets in the QGP [89]. More recently, Ref. [90] employed flexible quenching-weight parametrizations of the parton energy-loss distribution to analyze inclusive and photon-tagged jet measurements. Their GP-assisted Bayesian analysis examined whether a common energy-loss distribution could describe different hard processes and attempted to separate the quenching of quark- and gluon-initiated jets. The results supported an approximately universal description and indicated a gluon-to-quark energy-loss ratio somewhat larger than that expected from naive Casimir scaling. To further validate the closure tests, they examined whether the posterior distributions for the mean quark/gluon energy loss ⟨ϵi⟩\langle\epsilon_{i}\rangle and the color ratio CRC_{R} reproduce the true values used to generate the mock data. These quantities were derived from the posterior samples for each of the three parametrizations. As shown in Figure 6, the posterior distributions generally agree well with the true distributions across all parametrizations, confirming the reliability of their framework. However, closure tests showed that survival bias arising from the steeply falling jet spectrum strongly limits the reconstruction of the full energy-loss distribution and renders parts of the result sensitive to the assumed prior.

A more microscopic determination of the jet-medium interaction is via the extraction of the jet transport parameter q^=d⁡⟨k⟂2⟩/d​L\hat{q}=d\langle k_{\perp}^{2}\rangle/dL. Such studies were later carried out using microscopic transport models [91, 92]. A subsequent calibration included charged hadrons, DD mesons, and inclusive jets [93]. The authors introduced a closure-test metric related to the Kullback–Leibler divergence to quantify the information lost when a GP emulator replaces the full model. This metric was used to select the GP kernel and the number of retained principal components, as well as to identify parameters that were poorly reconstructed by the emulator. The work emphasized that emulator accuracy should be assessed through its effect on the inferred posterior, rather than only through pointwise prediction errors on a test set.

A subsequent analysis by the JETSCAPE Collaboration performed a joint calibration using inclusive-hadron and inclusive-jet suppression [94]. Because the required simulation campaign remained extremely expensive, the authors combined GP emulation with active learning. Starting from an initial space-filling design, the active-learning algorithm selected additional parameter points in regions of large emulator uncertainty, thereby allocating the available simulation budget more efficiently. The combined analysis constrained the virtuality- and temperature-dependent q^\hat{q}, but also revealed tensions between calibrations based on different subsets of the data. High-pTp_{T} hadrons and reconstructed jets yielded broadly compatible constraints, whereas lower-pTp_{T} hadrons preferred a different parameter region. The analysis traced this inconsistency primarily to the modeled dependence of q^\hat{q} on parton energy rather than to collision centrality. This is an important physical result: disagreements among posterior distributions inferred from different classes of observables can expose limitations of the model in different kinematic regions.

A complementary development addressed the prior dependence introduced by assuming a specific functional form for the temperature dependence of q^\hat{q}. Xie et al. treated q^​(T)\hat{q}(T) as an information field and constructed a nonparametric prior with controlled correlations over temperature [95, 96]. Unlike low-dimensional parametrizations, which can introduce artificial correlations between widely separated temperature regions, this formulation allows the data to constrain q^​(T)\hat{q}(T) primarily where they have sensitivity while leaving poorly probed regions prior dominated. Applied to a global analysis of single-hadron, dihadron, and photon–hadron measurements at RHIC and the LHC, the method yielded a pronounced temperature dependence of q^/T3\hat{q}/T^{3} and showed how measurements from different collision energies and centralities progressively constrain different temperature regions. This information-field approach therefore reduces functional-parametrization bias and makes the prior dependence of the extracted transport coefficient more transparent.

ML has also been used to determine which aspects of jet substructure carry the most information about medium modification. Lai et al. compared Particle Flow Networks, Energy Flow Networks, complete substructure bases, and sparse regression in distinguishing simulated jets in p​ppp and heavy-ion collisions [97]. They found that substantial discrimination power resides in soft and infrared- and collinear-unsafe information, but that much of this information is obscured by the fluctuating underlying event and can be further reduced by background subtraction. Sparse regression was then used to construct simpler observables that approximate the neural classifier while remaining more accessible to theoretical calculations.

III.4 Open heavy flavor and quarkonium

Open heavy flavor complements light hadrons and reconstructed jets by probing both partonic energy loss and the diffusion of heavy quarks through the QGP. The relevant quantities include the heavy-quark spatial diffusion coefficient Ds​(T,p)D_{s}(T,p), the momentum-broadening coefficient q^\hat{q}, and parameters controlling fragmentation and recombination.

An early Bayesian analysis calibrated an improved Langevin transport model to DD-meson RAAR_{\rm AA} and v2v_{2} data from RHIC and the LHC [98]. The analysis constrained the temperature and momentum dependence of 2​π​T​Ds2\pi TD_{s} and demonstrated that a common transport description could reproduce several collision systems. More recent analysis have increased both the physical scope and the statistical validation of this program.

A more recent analysis simultaneously inferred the temperature dependence of 2​π​T​Ds2\pi TD_{s} and q^/T3\hat{q}/T^{3} from DD-meson observables [99]. The study further constrained the ratio q^/κ\hat{q}/\kappa, where κ\kappa is the heavy-quark momentum-diffusion coefficient, and found a non-monotonic temperature dependence that deviates substantially from the naive expectation q^/κ=2\hat{q}/\kappa=2.

Heavy-flavor observables have also been used to constrain a broader description of the medium. Within a quasiparticle linear Boltzmann framework, Bayesian calibration to DD-meson RAAR_{\rm AA} and v2v_{2} was used to constrain both the effective coupling governing the QCD equation of state and the heavy-quark transport coefficient [100].

Quarkonium extends the hard-probe program from the transport of individual heavy quarks to the in-medium evolution of a correlated heavy-quark pair. A recent study parameterized the real and imaginary parts of the heavy-quark potential and propagated them through a time-dependent Schrödinger equation coupled to a hydrodynamic background [101]. Convolutional neural networks were trained as surrogates for the nonlinear map from the potential to bottomonium RAAR_{\rm AA} across several RHIC and LHC collision systems. Principal-component analysis and Gaussian-process regression were used to augment the training data, and stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics was then employed to sample the posterior distribution of the potential parameters. Within the adopted potential and medium model, the imaginary part was more strongly constrained and provided the dominant contribution to bottomonium suppression, whereas the inferred real part remained comparatively close to the vacuum Cornell form. This result is a strong example of ML entering several stages of a Bayesian workflow, although its physical interpretation must still be tested against variations of the hydrodynamic background, feed-down contributions, cold-nuclear-matter effects, and the functional form assumed for the potential.

III.5 Bayesian constraints on initial-state and pre-equilibrium dynamics

The early stage of a heavy-ion collision converts the structure of the incoming nuclei into the energy–momentum tensor and conserved-charge distributions that initialize the subsequent hydrodynamic evolution. Because this short-lived stage is not directly observable, its properties must be inferred from final-state measurements and are often correlated with the extracted transport properties of the QGP. Recent Bayesian studies have therefore moved beyond parameter estimation within a fixed dynamical model. They compare alternative descriptions of the initial state and pre-equilibrium evolution, examine theoretical consistency and causality, and propagate model and emulator uncertainties into the inferred posteriors. These developments help distinguish features of the early-time dynamics that are constrained by data from those that remain dependent on the assumed theoretical description.

Ref. [102] challenges the conventional practice of using parametric initial-condition models (e.g., TRENTo) by replacing them with SMASH (Simulating Many Accelerated Strongly-interacting Hadrons) transport to generate initial states for a (3+1)D viscous hydrodynamic + hadronic afterburner hybrid. The Bayesian analysis, calibrated to Pb–Pb collisions at sN​N=2.76\sqrt{s_{NN}}=2.76 TeV, reveals that transport-generated initial conditions produce significantly different posterior constraints on the specific shear viscosity (η/s\eta/s), which is an important transport coefficient for nuclear matter [103, 104, 105], compared to parametric models. Importantly, this work demonstrates that the initial-state modeling is not a mere nuisance, it directly couples to the extracted QGP properties. The physical, non-equilibrium-driven initial profiles lead to tighter constraints on early-time dynamics, implying that a more realistic description of the pre-hydrodynamic stage is essential for unbiased tomography of the QGP.

Ref. [106] addresses a fundamental theoretical issue: the validity of relativistic hydrodynamics in the early, far-from-equilibrium stage. The authors introduce causality constraints by penalizing or excluding regions in the evolution where the dissipative corrections violate the physically required conditions (e.g., positivity of the effective pressure or causality). Using a Bayesian analysis of flow observables in Au–Au collisions at RHIC, they find that imposing causality significantly shifts the posterior distributions of both the initial-condition parameters and the temperature-dependent specific bulk viscosity. The most striking result is that causality-violating parameter sets, which are statistically acceptable in standard analyses, become strongly disfavored once constraints are applied. This suggests that the early-time dynamics, when hydrodynamics is least justified, must be described by non-fluid approaches, otherwise, the inferred transport coefficients are biased by unphysical solutions. This paper directly quantifies how the frontier of the hydrodynamic description affects the entire Bayesian inference. Fig. 7 illustrates that specific shear and bulk viscosities as a function of temperature is biased by acausal regimes [106].

Ref. [107] introduces a rigorous framework for incorporating model discrepancy, the systematic error arising from the theoretical model itself—into the Bayesian analysis. Unlike standard approaches that assume the model can exactly describe reality with tuned parameters, this work explicitly models the discrepancy between the simulation output and actual experimental data using a Gaussian process. Applied to hadron spectra and flow in Pb–Pb collisions, the analysis shows that a significant portion of the data-model mismatch is absorbed by the discrepancy term rather than by parameter variation. Crucially, when model discrepancy is included, the inferred values of η/s\eta/s and the initial-state entropy deposition broaden substantially, and the early-time shear-stress tensor initialization parameters become less constrained. This implies that the theoretical uncertainty from the pre-equilibrium modeling is comparable to or larger than experimental and statistical uncertainties, and ignoring it leads to overconfident, potentially inaccurate parameter estimates.

In addition, there are also more sophisticated methods have been developed to model the initial stage and early-time evolution. Recent analyses have connected CGC initial conditions more directly to the soft observables measured in heavy-ion collisions. Heffernan et al. calibrated an IP-Glasma–hydrodynamics–hadronic-transport framework to Pb+Pb data [108, 109]. Transfer learning reduced the cost of constructing emulators for related model variants, while Bayesian model averaging propagated uncertainty associated with the hydrodynamic-to-hadronic transition. The analysis constrained both initial-state and QGP parameters and found that the available data did not statistically favor a temperature-dependent shear viscosity over a constant parametrization once model complexity was taken into account. The methodological advance here is therefore not only faster emulation, but also the use of ML-assisted transfer learning and Bayesian model averaging to treat differences among physical model choices.

III.6 Bayesian and machine-learning constraints on the nuclear initial state: from partonic structure to nuclear shape

The initial stages of high-energy nuclear collisions are controlled by the spatial and momentum distributions of quarks and gluons in the incoming nuclei. At small Bjorken xx, nonlinear gluon dynamics and event-by-event fluctuations determine the initial energy-density profile supplied to the subsequent pre-equilibrium and hydrodynamic evolution. Nuclear parton distribution functions, in contrast, provide the collinear partonic input for hard processes and cold-nuclear-matter baselines. Bayesian inference and ML enter these two problems differently: Bayesian calibration of Color Glass Condensate (CGC) calculations constrains model parameters and fluctuating geometry, while neural-network PDF analyses provide flexible functional parametrizations and data-driven uncertainty ensembles.

Bayesian methods have also been applied directly to the initial condition of small-xx evolution. Casuga, Karhunen, and Mäntysaari inferred parameters of the nonperturbative initial condition for the Balitsky–Kovchegov equation from HERA structure-function data [110]. A GP emulator and MCMC sampler made it possible to propagate the resulting posterior through the nonlinear evolution. The data favored an anomalous dimension close to unity, avoiding positivity problems encountered by some earlier parameter choices, and the posterior was propagated to proton–proton and future electron–ion observables. This is an important advance over a best-fit determination because it quantifies how uncertainty in the small-xx initial condition affects subsequent predictions.

A subsequent global analysis combined coherent and incoherent J/ψJ/\psi photoproduction on proton and lead targets [111]. Principal-component Gaussian-process emulators were trained on full CGC calculations, with additional training points selected from an intermediate posterior to improve accuracy in the high-likelihood region. This posterior-focused refinement is an elementary form of active learning. The study found that simultaneously describing proton and nuclear data remained difficult unless an additional normalization factor was introduced, thereby using Bayesian analysis to reveal model tension rather than only to determine parameter values. Such failures of posterior predictive agreement are physically informative because they identify missing ingredients in the assumed nuclear small-xx description.

Besides the parton-level wave function of the nuclei, relativistic nuclear collisions are increasingly used to study the nucleon-level structure of the colliding nuclei. Nuclear α\alpha-clustering structure [112, 113], nuclear radii, surface diffuseness, neutron skins, and intrinsic deformations influence the fluctuating initial geometry and are subsequently reflected in particle multiplicities, anisotropic flow, mean transverse momentum, and correlations among these observables [114, 115, 116, 117, 118]. Extracting nuclear structure from such measurements is nevertheless an inverse problem. In these applications, ML commonly enters through Gaussian-process (GP) emulators of the collision model or, more recently, through neural density estimators that directly approximate the posterior distribution.

A prominent application is the extraction of the neutron skin of Pb208{}^{208}\mathrm{Pb} from LHC data by Giacalone, Nijs, and van der Schee [119]. In this analysis, the neutron diffuseness was included among the parameters of a multistage heavy-ion collision model and constrained using observables in Pb–Pb collisions, together with the total p–Pb cross section. The observables included particle yields, mean transverse momenta, anisotropic-flow coefficients, and correlations between elliptic flow and mean transverse momentum. The resulting posterior yielded

Δ​rn​p​(Pb208)=0.217±0.058​fm,\Delta r_{np}({}^{208}\mathrm{Pb})=0.217\pm 0.058\penalty\ \mathrm{fm}, (9)

which was further translated into a constraint on the slope of the nuclear symmetry energy. An important methodological result was the identification of correlations between the neutron skin and parameters controlling the initial entropy deposition. This demonstrates why the nuclear and collision-model parameters should be inferred jointly rather than varied one at a time.

The sensitivity to nuclear deformation parameters was investigated by Cheng et al. using Bayesian imaging of Ru96+Ru96{}^{96}\mathrm{Ru}+{}^{96}\mathrm{Ru} and Zr96+Zr96{}^{96}\mathrm{Zr}+{}^{96}\mathrm{Zr} collisions [52]. The nuclear densities were parametrized by the Woods–Saxon radius RR, diffuseness aa, quadrupole deformation β2\beta_{2}, and octuple deformation β3\beta_{3}. A Monte Carlo Glauber model was evaluated at 1001 Latin-hypercube design points, after which principal-component analysis and GP emulation were used to interpolate its predictions. Posterior sampling was performed with the No-U-Turn Sampler, an adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm. Since the “data” in this study were generated by the same model, the analysis should be interpreted as a closure test rather than as an extraction from experimental measurements. It nevertheless established that multiplicity, elliptic and triangular eccentricities, and radial-size information provide complementary sensitivity to RR, aa, β2\beta_{2}, and β3\beta_{3}. It also showed that isobar ratios alone mainly constrain differences between the two nuclei and leave degeneracies in their absolute structures. Combining the ratios with selected single-system observables substantially improves the simultaneous reconstruction.

A more explicitly ML-based approach was introduced by Tao et al. for the inference of the quadrupole and hexadecapole deformations (β2,β4)(\beta_{2},\beta_{4}) from simulated heavy-ion initial states [75]. Permutation-invariant neural networks were used to encode ensembles of nucleon configurations or entropy-density profiles, while conditional normalizing flows learned the posterior directly from simulations. This constitutes simulation-based inference: the network is trained on parameter–simulation pairs without requiring an explicit analytic likelihood. The study found that aggregating information from multiple collision events is essential for suppressing event-by-event fluctuations. Quadrupole deformation was reconstructed more accurately than the weaker β4\beta_{4} signal, and central collisions carried more deformation information than peripheral collisions. Posterior coverage and probability-integral-transform tests were used to assess statistical calibration. This work demonstrates the potential of neural posterior estimation, although the analysis was restricted to simulated initial-state information and has not yet produced an extraction from final-state experimental data.

These examples illustrate a progression from model comparison, through GP-assisted Bayesian parameter estimation, to neural simulation-based inference of nuclear structure. At present, Bayesian extraction of more detailed structures, such as two-nucleon correlations or clustering, remains considerably less developed.

IV HIC Experiments with AI

Experimental uses of machine learning in heavy-ion physics differ from theory-side applications because the model can become part of the measurement chain. It must work with detector acceptance, pileup, backgrounds, high occupancy, finite resolution, calibration drift and online latency. The relevant quantities are therefore efficiency, resolution, stability over detector conditions, and the effect on final physics observables.

The QGP is extremely short-lived (approximately 10−2310^{-23} seconds) and cannot be observed directly, making its study one of the most challenging endeavors in modern nuclear physics. Traditional approaches rely on a combination of sophisticated theoretical models, computationally expensive numerical simulations, and statistical comparisons with experimental observables. This section presents selected examples of AI applications in heavy-ion collision experiments, organized into three thematic subsections.

IV.1 Jet Quenching Classification, Background Subtraction, and Unfolding

Jet quenching, i.e. the energy loss and modification of high-energy jets as they traverse the QGP, is one of the most powerful probes of the medium’s properties [120]. However, jet reconstruction in heavy-ion collisions suffers from a notoriously large and fluctuating thermal background. Reconstructed jets always include underlying event contamination, making it difficult to isolate genuine quenching effects from background-induced modifications [121].

Deep-learning methods have explored how more information can be recovered from individual jets. Haake and Loizides trained regressors using jet and constituent properties to estimate the hard jet momentum in the presence of a fluctuating heavy-ion background [122]. In simulation, the ML estimator achieved better momentum resolution than conventional area-based subtraction, particularly for low-pTp_{T} jets. This improvement could extend the kinematic reach of jet measurements, but its application to data requires validation against mismodeling of the background and the fragmentation pattern.

A major advance in this area is the use of machine learning to classify quenched jets on a jet-by-jet basis. Apolinário et al. established a rigorous baseline by embedding proton-proton jets into realistic heavy-ion backgrounds, ensuring that classification models learn to distinguish true QGP-induced modifications rather than background artifacts1 [46]. Their study demonstrated that a simple Boosted Decision Tree remains robust in scenarios where both medium response and underlying event are present, supporting portability to experimental contexts [46].

More sophisticated architectures have also been explored. Wu et al. employed Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks trained on jet substructure incorporating parton shower history to predict jet-by-jet quenching levels [123]. Using photon-jet samples from the Jewel event generator, they showed that LSTM predictions strongly correlate with true jet energy loss. The method was validated against Delphes detector simulations, confirming its ability to identify quenching effects in realistic environments [123].

Background subtraction itself has been revolutionized by deep learning. Qureshi and Kunnawalkam Elayavalli introduced DeepSub, the first machine learning-based approach for full-event background subtraction [124]. DeepSub utilizes a Swin Transformer-based model to denoise jet images and disentangle hard jets from the heavy-ion background. The method significantly outperforms existing subtraction techniques, reproducing key jet observables such as jet pTp_{T}, mass, and substructure observables at the sub-percent to percent level. Meanwhile, a Dense Neural Network (DNN) approach was developed to reconstruct jet momentum within a QGP background [125]. Training on quenched jets from the Linear Boltzmann Transport (LBT) model significantly reduced prediction bias compared to conventional Area-based and Constituent Subtraction methods.

Du, Pablos, and Tywoniuk used deep neural networks to estimate the initial, unquenched energy of a reconstructed jet from its final-state constituents [126]. Conditioning jet samples on the reconstructed initial energy reduces the survival bias associated with selecting jets by their final energy. In model studies, this procedure provided improved access to the spatial distribution and orientation of jet production and even allowed the production region of dijet pairs to be localized. The method therefore suggests a route toward event-by-event jet tomography, although the inferred initial energy and production geometry remain dependent on the jet-quenching model used to generate the training data.

Finally, measurements of jet observables are affected by detector-response smearing, with effects that are often correlated across multiple observables. Recent high-dimensional extensions of OmniFold have been developed to unfold jet measurements in the simultaneous presence of underlying-event background and detector effects [127]. Simulation studies showed that incorporating auxiliary information from up to 18 correlated observables can improve the unfolding of jet-substructure distributions.

IV.2 Real-Time Online Triggering and Data Processing with AI

Modern high-energy heavy-ion collision experiments face an extraordinary data challenge. At the ALICE experiment at the LHC, collisions occur at rates of up to 750,000 proton–proton collisions or 50,000 heavy-ion collisions per second [128]. In head-on heavy-ion collisions, thousands of particles can be produced simultaneously, creating exceptionally high track densities that must be reconstructed in real time. The ALICE detector produces data at rates of up to 1 terabyte per second, handled by a large online computing system equipped with around 2800 GPUs [128]. Under such extreme conditions, traditional data processing algorithms often become bottlenecks, and AI-based solutions have emerged as indispensable tools for real-time event selection, tracking, and reconstruction.

IV.2.1 Machine Learning-Based Online Triggers for Heavy-Flavor Event Selection

The sPHENIX experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) is designed to investigate the physics of the strongly coupled quark–gluon plasma (QGP) [121]. Heavy-flavor hadrons—containing charm and beauty quarks—serve as key probes of the QGP produced during heavy-ion collisions. However, the production rates of heavy-flavor events are notably low: in p+p collisions at s\sqrt{s} = 200 GeV, charm and beauty events account for only 0.3% and 0.003%, respectively. Compounding this challenge, the sPHENIX detector’s readout event rate is limited to 15 kHz due to constraints in the outer calorimeter readout system, meaning the experiment can collect only approximately 0.5% of full detector data [121].

To overcome this limitation, a dedicated online trigger system based on machine learning has been developed. The algorithms, primarily built on Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and Bipartite Graph Neural Networks (BGNN), use only spatial track hit information from fast silicon detectors as input. This design choice is critical for online deployment—the algorithm must make decisions within extremely tight latency constraints, and using minimal, low-level detector information reduces computational overhead. Evaluated on Monte Carlo simulations of charm-quark events in p+p collisions at s\sqrt{s} = 200 GeV, the system achieves a track reconstruction efficiency of 0.945, with precision and recall for identifying heavy-flavor events both around 0.79. This work demonstrates that graph-based neural architectures can effectively identify rare heavy-flavor signatures in real time, significantly enhancing the physics reach of the sPHENIX experiment despite its readout rate limitations. Fig. 8 illustrates that the flow-chart to identify HF quark events [121].

A related end-to-end AI-enabled triggering solution has been developed for relativistic heavy-ion colliders and future Electron-Ion Colliders [129]. This system, based on Graph Neural Networks, classifies trigger events versus background events, makes online decisions to retain signal data, and enables efficient data acquisition. The integration of GNNs into the trigger chain represents a paradigm shift: rather than relying on hand-crafted thresholds and cuts, the system learns directly from data to distinguish signal from background, adapting to the complex correlations present in high-multiplicity heavy-ion events.

IV.2.2 CNN-Based Online Trigger for QGP Event Selection

A complementary approach to online triggering focuses on directly selecting events associated with QGP formation. Soloveva et al. developed a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based trigger concept that encodes events as compact multidimensional histograms of reconstructed particle content, including particle species, momentum magnitude, and angular information. The method was first evaluated within the Parton-Hadron-String Dynamics (PHSD) framework, where microscopic QGP-related labels are available, and independently validated against Ultra-relativistic Quantum Molecular Dynamics (UrQMD) simulations [120].

For realistic deployment, a lightweight C++ inference package, ANN4FLES, is employed at the physics-analysis stage after tracking and topology reconstruction. For Au+Au collisions at 30 AGeV, the classification accuracy decreases from 95.1% on generator-level PHSD events to 83.7% after full reconstruction, while retaining practical separation power for online event selection. Importantly, SHAP-based interpretability analysis was used to identify the dominant particle-species contributions to the network decision, providing physics insight into what the network has learned. This work illustrates a key advantage of AI-based triggers: not only do they perform the selection task, but they can also be interrogated to reveal which physical features drive their decisions [120].

IV.2.3 Neural Networks for Real-Time Cluster Finding and Track Reconstruction

Beyond event-level triggering, AI is being deployed at the lowest levels of data processing—the reconstruction of individual detector signals. In October 2025, the ALICE Collaboration deployed, for the first time, a neural-network-based algorithm for real-time processing in the experiment [130]. Its purpose is to reconstruct clusters from the raw readout of the Time Projection Chamber (TPC)—small groups of signals generated as charged particles traverse the detector. These clusters form the fundamental input for particle tracking.

The challenge is substantial: in head-on heavy-ion collisions, thousands of charged particles are produced simultaneously, and their signals in the TPC can overlap significantly. The neural network not only reconstructs clusters but also assigns to each a probability that it originates either from background noise or from a real particle traversing the detector. This approach effectively acts as a smart filter that removes noise and separates overlapping features, producing a cleaner, more interpretable representation of the event. The deployment of this algorithm marks a significant milestone—it demonstrates that neural networks can operate within the extreme computational constraints of real-time data processing at the LHC, using smaller models and lower numerical precision optimized for specific hardware.

A Graph Neural Network with attention mechanism and two-stage aggregation has also been developed for particle track reconstruction in the Time-Projection Chamber of the MPD detector at the NICA accelerator complex [131]. These developments highlight a broader trend: tracking and clustering tasks, which are both highly complex and naturally parallelizable, are particularly well-suited for machine learning approaches. Previously developed algorithms have now been matched or surpassed in their performance by trainable approaches such as neural networks. For instance, an example of track reconstruction results obtained using the GNN model and projected onto the xy-plane was shown in Fig. 9.

IV.2.4 Contrastive Metric Learning for Stable Shower Reconstruction

Recently, a new AI-powered event-processing algorithm is being readied to cope with the torrent of data that will stream from the Large Hadron Collider upgrade [132, 133]. The work presents a clustering framework for point cloud segmentation in high-granularity calorimeters based on supervised contrastive metric learning (CML). Unlike object-centric approaches that predict cluster assignments or condensation points, CML learns a latent embedding space where hits from the same particle shower are pulled together while hits from different showers are pushed apart. Clustering is performed as a separate post-training readout using a density-based procedure, decoupling representation learning from cluster formation.

The method is rigorously compared against object condensation (OC) using identical graph neural network backbones and matched embedding dimensionality on simulated electromagnetic and hadronic shower datasets.
