Geometric analysis reveals that CML produces narrow and stable separation margin distributions, whereas OC yields broad and often negative margins, indicating intrinsic ambiguity in clustering decisions. Fig. 10 demonstrates the event-level embedding-geometry distributions for simulated electro-magnetic (EM) and hadronic (HAD) showers at increasing generated particle multiplicity (Np​a​r​t​i​c​l​e​sN_{particles}). This geometric advantage translates directly into superior reconstruction performance: CML achieves higher efficiency, higher purity, more stable multiplicity ratios, and improved energy resolution, with the largest gains observed at high multiplicities where shower overlap is most severe.

In mixed-particle training scenarios, CML maintains consistent performance across particle types, while OC degrades substantially, particularly for electromagnetic showers. The results demonstrate that learning a similarity-based representation with a stable geometric structure is more effective than optimizing object-centric clustering variables for dense point cloud segmentation. The authors conclude that contrastive metric learning combined with density-based readout offers a robust and promising alternative to object-centric methods for reconstruction in highly granular detectors, with potential applicability beyond high-energy physics to general point cloud segmentation problems where object boundaries are ambiguous and overlap is common.

V Holographic QCD with machine learning

The Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence [134, 135, 136], more broadly referred to as holographic duality, has become one of the central frameworks for studying strongly coupled quantum many-body systems. Its core idea is that certain quantum field theories can be equivalently described by a gravitational theory in one higher dimension. In practice, this duality provides an alternative language for non-perturbative dynamics: difficult field-theory questions may be translated into geometric problems in the bulk spacetime. Over the past two decades, this perspective has had a major impact not only in high-energy theory, but also in condensed matter physics, hydrodynamics, and quantum information.

For QCD and QCD-like theories, holography is especially attractive because many of the most important phenomena of interest—confinement, chiral symmetry breaking, real-time transport, and finite-density dynamics—occur precisely in regimes where perturbation theory is unreliable. Since a fully controlled top-down holographic dual of real QCD is not available, much of the phenomenological progress has relied on effective bottom-up constructions. These include hard-wall and soft-wall AdS/QCD [137, 138, 139], improved holographic QCD [140, 141], Einstein-dilaton and Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton models [142, 143], and V-QCD/Einstein-Dilaton-Flavor-type models [144]. Related top-down or string-inspired constructions, such as the Sakai–Sugimoto model [145, 146], have also provided important guidance. These frameworks have been remarkably successful at reproducing qualitative and even semi-quantitative features of hadron physics and the quark-gluon plasma. At the same time, traditional model building often depends on phenomenological ansätze for the warp factor, dilaton profile, or coupling functions, which introduces an element of arbitrariness.

Machine learning provides a systematic way to constrain this model-building freedom with data. As illustrated in Fig. 11, conventional forward modeling starts from a specified bulk model and compares its predictions with experimental or lattice results, whereas ML-assisted inference uses boundary observables to constrain model parameters or reconstruct bulk functions, which then serve as the basis for further predictions [147]. This shifts the emphasis toward data-driven inference without eliminating model dependence; physical constraints and uncertainty quantification therefore remain important. The resulting research program may be organized into several interconnected directions, ranging from conceptual links between renormalization and deep learning to concrete applications in spectroscopy, thermodynamics, quarkonium physics, proton structure, and transport.

V.1 From Renormalization Group to Deep Generative Models

An important intellectual precursor to ML-assisted holography is the long-recognized relation between the renormalization group (RG) and the extra radial dimension in AdS. In holography, the radial coordinate is naturally interpreted as an energy scale, with the ultraviolet (UV) boundary corresponding to short-distance physics and the infrared (IR) interior encoding long-distance dynamics [148]. This picture suggests that the emergent bulk geometry may be understood as a geometric representation of coarse graining.

This RG/geometric intuition is also closely related to tensor-network approaches to holography, where entanglement renormalization and MERA provide discrete realizations of an emergent radial direction [149]. In this broader context, deep learning offers another hierarchical language for representing coarse graining and latent bulk degrees of freedom. Early influential works [150, 151] argued that neural-network architectures can be viewed as concrete realizations of holographic or RG-like structures. In Ref. [150], the hierarchical organization of a deep neural network (DNN) was interpreted as an RG flow, and it was suggested that repeated coarse graining naturally generates a hyperbolic geometry reminiscent of AdS. In this RG/geometric intuition, the depth of the network plays the role of the holographic direction, while the compression of information across layers mirrors the flow from UV degrees of freedom to effective IR descriptions.

A closely related probabilistic formulation was proposed in Ref. [151], where the AdS/CFT correspondence was mapped to a deep Boltzmann machine (DBM). In that construction, visible units represent the boundary field-theory variables and hidden units represent bulk degrees of freedom distributed along the radial direction. The network energy function is associated with the bulk action, and the boundary generating functional is obtained by integrating over hidden variables. This is conceptually important because it recasts holography as a generative model: the bulk acts as a latent representation from which boundary configurations are produced.

These ideas were further developed in more explicitly constructive directions. Ref. [152] proposed a neural-network renormalization-group algorithm based on flow-type generative models. The goal was to learn an exact holographic mapping between uncorrelated bulk variables and the interacting boundary field ensemble. When applied to the critical regime of a two-dimensional complex ϕ4\phi^{4} theory, the learned geometry of the latent manifold was found to be consistent with a three-dimensional hyperbolic space, providing numerical evidence that an AdS-like structure can emerge from data-driven learning.

Taken together, these studies established a conceptual bridge between RG, information compression, and generative learning. They also motivated a broader perspective that has become central in recent years: holography may be viewed not only as a formal duality, but also as an inverse-learning problem in which geometry is inferred from observables. This conceptual relation is summarized schematically in Fig. 12, which juxtaposes the RG interpretation of the AdS radial direction with the DBM picture of hidden bulk layers.

V.2 Methodological Core: Geometric Reconstruction and Holographic Inverse Problems

The most direct and influential line of work concerns the inverse problem itself: how to reconstruct a bulk spacetime, an effective action, or a set of coupling functions from boundary data. This direction forms the methodological backbone of the field, because essentially all later phenomenological applications rely on the ability to infer holographic models from observables rather than specifying them a priori. A central difficulty, however, is that holographic reconstruction is generally non-unique: different bulk potentials, coordinate choices, or matter couplings may reproduce the same limited set of boundary observables. The role of modern ML architectures is therefore not only to fit data efficiently, but also to incorporate physical priors, constraints, and uncertainty estimates that make the inverse problem better posed.

V.2.1 Foundational frameworks and early works

A first concrete realization of this program appeared in the so-called AdS/deep learning correspondence [153, 154]. In these studies, the radial evolution of bulk fields was represented by a deep neural network whose layers correspond to discretized positions in the bulk. Network weights were identified with geometric quantities such as metric components or interaction terms. By training on boundary observables, the network was able to reconstruct a bulk background that reproduces the data. A notable feature of these early models was that geometrically meaningful structures, such as a black-hole horizon, could emerge from the training procedure rather than being imposed from the beginning. This marked a qualitative shift from forward modeling to inverse reconstruction.

V.2.2 Algorithmic refinements and physically informed architectures

Subsequent studies improved both the numerical stability and the physical transparency of the reconstruction. One important step was the introduction of Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) [155, 156]. In contrast to discrete-layer networks, Neural ODEs treat the network depth as a continuous variable. This is especially natural in holography, where the radial direction is itself continuous. In practice, the method allows one to model the radial evolution of bulk fields or metric functions by solving trainable differential equations, reducing discretization artifacts and making the learned geometry smoother. These approaches have been used, for example, to reconstruct temperature-dependent holographic backgrounds more efficiently and to improve the extraction of thermodynamic quantities [156]. Related pedagogical introductions to the AdS/deep-learning correspondence are given in [157].

Another major development is the use of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [158, 159, 160]. In PINN-based frameworks, the loss function is not based solely on matching data. It also contains residuals of the bulk equations of motion, such as Einstein equations, dilaton equations, or constraint equations. This makes the learned solution more interpretable and better aligned with the underlying theory. Instead of fitting observables in a purely black-box fashion, PINNs enforce that the reconstructed geometry is dynamically consistent. This is particularly useful when the available boundary data are limited, because the field equations provide a strong inductive bias. PINNs have also been applied to forward holographic calculations, for example to compute holographic entanglement entropy and entanglement-wedge cross sections for prescribed asymptotically AdS geometries [161].

A complementary variational strategy has also emerged in holographic flavor physics. Instead of enforcing the Euler–Lagrange equations through residual losses, one may parameterize a probe-brane embedding by a neural network and directly minimize the regularized DBI action, interpreted as a thermodynamic free energy. This action-level formulation is particularly natural in flavor-brane systems, where the physical embedding is selected through an extremization principle. It provides a useful counterpart to PINN-based reconstruction: while PINNs enforce the equations of motion through differential residuals, the variational approach imposes the underlying extremization principle directly at the level of the action [162].

More recently, new architectures have been explored for specific tasks. Transformer-based models [163] have been used in settings where one aims to predict geometric information from nonlocal quantum data such as entanglement entropy. Since transformers are well suited to learning long-range correlations, they are natural candidates for reconstructing bulk features encoded in multipartite boundary information. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) [164] and related KAN-based holographic parametrizations [165] are also attracting interest because they can yield more interpretable functional relations than standard multilayer perceptrons. In holographic reconstruction, this raises the possibility of obtaining approximate analytic forms for bulk potentials or coupling functions, rather than only numerical outputs.

V.2.3 Boundary observables used as training data

An important sign of maturity in this area is the diversity of observables now used as inputs. Early studies often focused on relatively simple thermodynamic or condensate data, but later work showed that the inverse problem can be posed using a broad range of boundary information. These inputs may be roughly organized into local equilibrium observables, real-time response functions, nonlocal probes, and hadronic structure observables. Each class constrains a different aspect of the holographic model. Thermodynamic data mainly fix the equilibrium black-hole background; transport and conductivity data are sensitive to near-horizon dynamics and matter couplings; entanglement entropy, Wilson loops, and static potentials probe extended bulk geometry and IR confinement physics; hadronic structure functions instead constrain bulk hadron wave functions and exchange kernels relevant for deep-inelastic scattering.

Real-time response data provide one class of input. For example, shear viscosity and related dissipative quantities were considered in [166], while optical conductivity was used in [167, 168]. In such cases, the reconstructed geometry is constrained by the requirement that it reproduces frequency-dependent response functions, which are sensitive to both the near-horizon region and the bulk matter couplings.

Another important input comes from quantum information observables. Entanglement entropy [169, 170] has been employed in [171, 163, 172] as a probe of bulk geometry, motivated by the fact that holographic entanglement directly relates boundary entanglement patterns to extremal surfaces in the bulk. These studies are conceptually significant because they connect data-driven reconstruction to the broader idea that spacetime geometry is encoded in quantum information.

Nonlocal observables such as Wilson loops and static quark-antiquark potentials have also been used [173, 165]. Since these probes are particularly sensitive to confinement physics and the IR structure of the geometry, they complement thermodynamic inputs that primarily constrain the equilibrium black-hole background.

A related extension concerns hadronic structure functions. Ref. [174] introduced a physics-guided neural network for the proton structure function F2F_{2} in holographic QCD, embedding the AdS5 Dirac equation and the holographic string-diffusion kernel directly into the learning architecture. This illustrates how physics-integrated learning can extend holographic QCD beyond thermodynamics and spectroscopy toward deep-inelastic scattering and the transition between resonance-dominated and diffractive regimes.

Finally, equation-of-state data and other thermodynamic observables remain central ingredients in many reconstruction programs [159]. Overall, this methodological direction has evolved from proof-of-principle demonstrations into a flexible toolbox of inverse solvers. It now combines neural architectures, differential-equation solvers, and explicit physical constraints, thereby providing the technical foundation for data-driven holographic phenomenology.

V.3 Vacuum Structure and Hadron Spectroscopy

A second major application area concerns the vacuum structure of QCD and the spectroscopy of hadronic states. Here the goal is to reproduce hadronic observables associated with confinement, chiral symmetry breaking, and bound-state spectra, and then to infer the corresponding bulk background or action.

In soft-wall and related AdS/QCD models, hadron masses depend sensitively on the warp factor and dilaton profile. This makes spectroscopy a natural target for inverse reconstruction. Refs. [175, 176], for example, used meson spectral data such as the ρ\rho and a2a_{2} trajectories to reconstruct effective holographic backgrounds or dilaton potentials. More recent extensions have considered broader unflavoured meson spectra, including scalar, vector, axial-vector, and tensor channels [177]. The basic strategy is to determine bulk functions in such a way that the eigenvalue problem for normalizable bulk modes reproduces the observed Regge-like structure of meson masses. This line of work demonstrates that ML can extract effective backgrounds directly from hadronic data, reducing the need for hand-tuned soft-wall profiles.

The reconstruction can be further pushed in Einstein-dilaton, IHQCD-type, and soft-wall-inspired settings. In such constructions, one often seeks to determine not only the background solution but also the dilaton profile or potential, because these functions control the running coupling, confinement scale, and IR physics of the theory. Studies such as [178, 177, 179] used chiral condensates, unflavoured meson spectra, or heavy-quarkonium spectra as inputs to infer the shape of the dilaton sector. In this sense, the problem shifts from fitting a background to learning part of the holographic action. This is a more ambitious inverse problem, since multiple sectors of observables may have to be reproduced simultaneously.

An especially interesting development is the attempt to unify vacuum spectroscopy with finite-temperature physics in a single model. Ref. [180] is an example of this trend. Fig. 13 illustrates the sequential stages of the holographic reconstruction workflow. The process begins with the transformation of glueball spectra data into the reconstructed metric potential Vg​(z)V_{g}(z) via Schrödinger inversion. From this, the composite derivative function Bp​(Z)=3​A′​(z)−Ψ′​(z)B_{p}(Z)=3A^{\prime}(z)-\Psi^{\prime}(z) is extracted through potential decomposition. The workflow concludes by integrating equation-of-state (EOS) constraints with the derived Bp​(z)B_{p}(z) to reconstruct the warp factor A⁡(z)A(z). With the neural-network parametrization of A⁡(z)A(z) constrained by both the EOS and the glueball spectrum, the entropy density is computed and compared against lattice results, showing good agreement.

There, an ML-assisted Einstein-dilaton model was constrained at the same time by lattice thermodynamic data and by the scalar glueball spectrum of pure Yang-Mills theory. The significance of this result is not only technical but conceptual: it suggests that finite-temperature thermodynamics and zero-temperature bound-state physics can be described consistently within one reconstructed background, rather than by separate models specialized to different observables.

More broadly, this direction shows that data-driven holography can reverse-engineer the non-perturbative QCD vacuum from phenomenology. Rather than treating hadron spectroscopy and confinement diagnostics as qualitative benchmarks, the newer literature uses them as quantitative constraints on the effective five-dimensional theory.

V.4 QCD Thermodynamics and the Phase Diagram

Finite-temperature and finite-density QCD is arguably the most active arena for ML-assisted holographic model building. The central goal is to calibrate a holographic effective theory against reliable lattice-QCD data at vanishing baryon chemical potential and then use the model to extrapolate into the finite-density region, where lattice methods face severe difficulties.

A common starting point is to fit the QCD equation of state, including quantities such as pressure, entropy density, trace anomaly, and baryon-number susceptibilities. In this context, Einstein-Dilaton-Flavor models [181] incorporate the effects of 2+12+1 dynamical flavors and allow one to address both thermodynamic and chiral observables. By optimizing model parameters with ML tools, such constructions can reproduce the lattice crossover behavior and study how the phase structure varies with quark masses, including applications to the Columbia plot. Related EMD-plus-flavor constructions [182] have used neural-ODE reconstruction and back-reaction tests to constrain the QCD equation of state from lattice data.

Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton models provide another widely used framework [183, 184]. In these models, the metric and dilaton encode the gluonic sector, while a bulk gauge field captures the effects of baryon chemical potential. ML-based reconstruction is used to infer metric functions and gauge-dilaton couplings from lattice input. Fully data-driven EMD realizations such as Refs. [184, 185] represent the warp factor and gauge-dilaton coupling by neural networks and learn these functions directly from lattice or hadron-resonance-gas data. Complementary approaches retain analytical holographic ansätze and use machine learning or gradient-based optimization to calibrate their parameters against lattice data [147, 186].

Once calibrated at μB=0\mu_{B}=0, these models can be continued to finite baryon chemical potential, where holography becomes especially valuable. Several studies have used ML-assisted holographic models to explore the possible emergence and location of the QCD critical endpoint in the (T,μB)(T,\mu_{B}) plane [184, 185, 186], while its dependence on the number of flavors has been investigated explicitly in Ref. [147]. Although different model assumptions lead to different numerical values, the broader significance is that the CEP search can be formulated as a constrained inference problem rather than a purely phenomenological scan.

External magnetic fields add another layer of complexity. Ref. [187] used Neural ODE techniques to investigate the phase diagram in the presence of strong magnetic fields. Figure 14 illustrates the neural ODE workflow. Boundary conditions are imposed at the ultraviolet (UV) boundary and the black hole event horizon. The neural ODE numerically solves the equations of motion to produce a trial equation of state, which is iteratively optimized via backpropagation to minimize deviations from lattice QCD data. This procedure efficiently converges to an optimal magnetic coupling, yielding good agreement with lattice data and enabling model predictions across unexplored magnetic fields and chemical potentials. The resulting phase structure can become considerably richer, with indications of nontrivial critical behavior and even the possibility of multiple critical endpoints in some parameter regimes. Such results illustrate how flexible neural reconstruction methods are in extending holographic models beyond standard thermodynamic settings.

A particularly important advance is the incorporation of uncertainty quantification. Bayesian approaches [188, 189] allow one to infer posterior distributions for model parameters and derived observables rather than quoting only a single best-fit result. In practice, this means that one can attach credible intervals to the predicted equation of state, the phase boundary, or the CEP location. For a field that historically relied heavily on model intuition, this is a major step toward statistical rigor.

In summary, ML has substantially strengthened the role of holographic QCD in finite-temperature and finite-density phenomenology. It enables efficient calibration to lattice data, facilitates extrapolation into otherwise inaccessible regions of the phase diagram, and increasingly supports uncertainty-controlled predictions.

V.5 Heavy Quarkonium in the Quark-Gluon Plasma

Heavy quarkonia, especially charmonium and bottomonium, are among the most informative probes [190] of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). Because the heavy quark mass introduces a relatively hard scale, quarkonium states can survive above the deconfinement crossover for some temperature range, and their eventual melting encodes valuable information about in-medium screening and dissipation. Holographically, these systems are often studied either through spectral functions computed in thermal black-hole backgrounds or through Wilson-loop and static-potential observables. This builds on earlier holographic studies of meson melting and thermal spectral functions in flavor-brane constructions [191, 192].

Beyond spectral functions, Ref. [193] used a Bayesian holographic QCD model calibrated to lattice-QCD thermodynamic data to study heavy-quarkonium thermodynamic observables, including the interquark distance, potential energy, entropy, binding energy, and internal energy at finite temperature and baryon chemical potential. This provides an uncertainty-aware, potential-based description of how the hot and dense medium affects quarkonium dissociation.

Related potential-based work includes Ref. [194], which used a machine-learned holographic background to extract the complex static quarkonium potential and the temperature dependence of the dissociation length. A complementary spectral-function analysis was carried out in Ref. [195], where a data-driven EMD background was combined with a heavy-quark probe sector to study charmonium and bottomonium dissociation at finite temperature and baryon chemical potential. Together with related anisotropic spectral-function studies [196], this work supports a common qualitative pattern: excited states are more fragile than ground states, spectral peaks broaden and decrease in height as the medium becomes hotter or denser, and anisotropy can enhance dissociation. This sequential pattern, in which excited states such as 2S modes melt before the corresponding 1S ground states, is qualitatively consistent with the standard sequential-suppression picture of quarkonium in a hot medium.

This direction is important because it moves holographic QCD beyond equilibrium bulk thermodynamics and toward in-medium hard-probe dynamics. Spectral functions, complex potentials, screening lengths, and dissociation temperatures provide complementary diagnostics that are closer to heavy-ion phenomenology than the equation of state alone. As a result, quarkonium studies provide a testing ground for whether data-driven holographic models can describe not only the equation of state of the plasma but also the fate of hard probes embedded in it.

V.6 Transport Properties of the Quark-Gluon Plasma

Depending on the workflow, transport observables can either be used as inputs for reconstruction or treated as predictions after the equilibrium background has been calibrated. Once a holographic background has been calibrated to reproduce thermodynamic data, it becomes possible to compute a wide class of transport coefficients and hard-probe observables [197, 198, 199, 200]. This is one of the most practical advantages of holography, because real-time transport is difficult to obtain from first principles in QCD, especially at finite density.

Ref. [201] used a KAN-based holographic background to compute the heavy-quark drag force, the jet-quenching parameter, and the heavy-quark diffusion coefficient. Ref. [202] extended this program to a Bayesian holographic setting, calculating these hard-probe observables together with shear and bulk viscosities while propagating posterior uncertainty. These observables are obtained from probe-string configurations and bulk fluctuation equations in the reconstructed geometry. Near-horizon data play a central role for several transport coefficients, while the full radial background can also enter hard-probe observables. What is new in the ML-assisted setting is that these transport predictions are made on top of backgrounds that have already been quantitatively constrained by lattice or phenomenological data.

An especially promising step is the use of Bayesian methods in transport calculations [202]. Rather than providing a single curve for each coefficient, the analysis propagates model uncertainty into the transport sector and reports credible intervals, for example at the 68% and 95% levels. This makes it possible to compare holographic predictions more meaningfully with lattice estimates and phenomenological constraints extracted from heavy-ion measurements, including ALICE data. Even when the uncertainties are still substantial, the framework represents a clear improvement over purely deterministic model fitting.

This line of work highlights the predictive potential of data-driven holography. Once a model has been trained on equilibrium observables, one can use it as a “holographic simulator” to infer real-time properties that are difficult to measure directly and difficult to calculate in traditional approaches. In that sense, transport studies are where the practical value of the entire reconstruction program becomes visible.

V.7 Short Summary and Outlook

The combination of machine learning and holographic QCD has developed into a coherent research program with a recognizable methodological core and a rapidly expanding range of applications. Conceptually, it builds on the common logic of RG flow, emergent geometry, and hierarchical latent representations. Methodologically, it formulates holographic model building as an inverse problem in which bulk geometries, matter couplings, or effective actions are inferred from boundary observables. Phenomenologically, it now spans vacuum spectroscopy, finite-temperature and finite-density thermodynamics, proton structure, heavy-quarkonium dynamics, and plasma transport.

The main challenge is no longer simply whether neural networks can fit holographic data, but whether the reconstructed bulk structures are unique, physically interpretable, and predictive outside the training regime. Future progress will likely require richer datasets, stronger theoretical priors, transparent architectures, and systematic uncertainty quantification. In this sense, ML-assisted holographic QCD is moving the field from qualitative model building toward a more constrained and uncertainty-aware framework for strong-coupling phenomenology.

VI Neutron Star

Neutron stars probe QCD matter in a regime complementary to the QGP produced in heavy-ion collisions: the matter is cold, beta-equilibrated and in macroscopic gravitational equilibrium, strongly interacting, and compressed to several times nuclear saturation density. The main physics unknown is the dense-matter EoS, usually represented as a relation among pressure, energy density, baryon density, and composition [203, 204, 205]. Observations do not measure this relation directly. Instead, they constrain neutron stars’ masses, radii, tidal deformabilities, moments of inertia, cooling behavior, and gravitational-wave signals, which are indirect functions of the EoS. The theoretical task is therefore an inverse problem: infer an EoS from observables after passing through the TOV equations and, for mergers, dynamical simulations, while ensuring that the physical constraints to be satisfied, such as stability, causality, and high-density asymptotic behavior, are respected.

VI.1 Neural EoS Reconstruction

Traditional neutron-star inference uses parameterized EoS families or non-parametric Bayesian priors and confronts them with astrophysical likelihoods. ML adds complementary strategies for representing functions, generating admissible EoS ensembles, and accelerating inverse maps. Early deep-learning studies learned direct maps from neutron-star observables to the underlying EoS [206, 207]. This direct inversion view is simple and fast, but it is sensitive to the assumed training ensemble. Subsequent work has therefore paid more attention to uncertainty quantification, data augmentation, and the use of probability distributions instead of isolated measurements [208]. In this line of work, the main question is no longer whether a network can reproduce a test set. The question is which part of the inferred EoS is actually constrained by the data.

Generative models give another way to organize the EoS space. Conditional variational-autoencoders can reconstruct pressure curves from a set of mass-radius observations after training on physically filtered EoS samples [209]. Structured variational autoencoders can also separate supervised stellar quantities, such as Mm​a​xM_{max} and R1.4R_{1.4}, from additional latent variables that describe residual EoS freedom. [210]. Figure 15 shows this idea. The latent variables are not physical observables by themselves, but they provide a compact coordinate system for generating and testing EoS candidates. These studies clarify that ML inference is meaningful only when trained on physically admissible EoS ensembles and tested against distribution shifts.

A more physics-driven direction represents the EoS itself by a neural network and couples it to the differentiable stellar-structure equations’ solver. Neural reconstruction from mass-radius or tidal data has been developed using automatic differentiation (AD) and trained TOV-solver networks [211, 212]. Ref. [211] demonstrated the devised AD-based neural reconstruction on mock data, and Ref. [212] applied this method to the accumulated mass-radius real observations. Figure. 16 illustrates the workflow where known physical equations define the map from a candidate EoS to the observable space. Ref. [213] used automatic differentiation to invert the TOV solving more explicitly and discussed the possibility to identify possible first-order phase transition for dense QCD matter. In this setting, a neural network represents the EoS, the TOV equations map it to mass-radius data, and gradients are back-propagated through the solver. The advantage is conceptual as well as computational: the learning problem is tied to the known physical equations, rather than replacing them by a black-box map.

Recent work has moved from point reconstruction toward posterior inference via deep learning. Neural simulation-based inference can infer the EoS directly from telescope spectra [74], while normalizing flows provide rapid posterior sampling for neutron-star EoS constraints [214]. Deep-learning EoS inference has also been studied in settings designed to include realistic observational uncertainties [215]. Simulation-based inference can be combined with universal relations to improve accuracy and reduce the dimensional burden of the inference problem [216]. These methods are attractive because they can handle non-Gaussian and correlated posteriors, which are common when masses, radii, and tidal deformabilities constrain overlapping but not identical density ranges.

A persistent difficulty is that the high-density EoS is not uniquely determined by present data. Many EoS curves can satisfy the observed two-solar-mass constraint, produce compatible radii, and yield similar tidal deformabilities. ML does not remove this degeneracy; instead, it can expose and quantify it. Physical constraints must therefore be built into the inference. At low density the EoS should be consistent with nuclear theory, at high density it should not violate causality or thermodynamic stability, and in between it may allow rapid changes associated with new degrees of freedom or phase transitions. Recent studies have used Bayesian and neural approaches to search for possible QCD phase transitions in neutron-star interiors [213], and anomaly-detection ideas have been proposed to identify unusual EoS behavior in neural inference [217].

VI.2 Physical constraints

Present observations do not determine a unique high-density EoS. Many curves satisfy the two-solar-mass constraint, produce compatible radii, and yield similar tidal deformabilities. Machine Learning can expose and quantify this degeneracy, but it cannot eliminate it by itself. Its useful role is to show which density ranges remain uncertain and how the answer changes with priors, data choices, and physical filters. Physical constraints must therefore be built into the inference. At low density, the EoS should be consistent with nuclear theory. At high density, it must respect causality, thermodynamic stability and perturbative QCD results. At intermediate densities, rapid changes in the speed of sound may indicate new degrees of freedom or phase transitions.

This makes neutron-star inference a natural testing ground for uncertainty-aware Machine Learning. Bayesian and automatic differentiation neural network approaches have been used to search for possible QCD phase transitions in neutron-star interiors [213], and anomaly-detection ideas have been proposed to identify unusual EoS behavior in neural inference [217]. Symbolic regression provides a complementary, interpretable route by learning compact relations between neutron-star observables and nuclear-matter properties [218, 219]. The defensible output is a calibrated statement about which classes of EoS behavior remain compatible with the data and priors, rather than a unique claim about core composition.

VI.3 Connections to HICs

The connection to heavy-ion physics is important but subtle. Heavy-ion collisions and neutron stars probe different thermodynamic trajectories of the QCD phase diagram: hot and dynamical matter in one case, cold and beta-equilibrated matter in the other. A direct merger of information from the two sets is therefore not automatic. Nevertheless, both are sensitive to the same underlying strong-interaction physics at finite baryon density. Huth et al. performed a joint analysis of heavy-ion constraints, multimessenger observations, and microscopic theory to constrain neutron-star matter [220]. The relevant complementarity is physical: heavy-ion dynamics and stellar structure respond to overlapping aspects of the strong interaction, but in different temperature and isospin regimes. A relation inferred for approximately symmetric matter in a collision cannot simply be identified with the cold betaequilibrated stellar EoS.

A promising long-term direction is a joint inference framework in which heavy-ion data, neutron-star observations, chiral effective theory, perturbative QCD constraints, and lattice information at small chemical potential are treated as complementary constraints on dense QCD matter. For such a program, ML is useful not primarily as a fitting device, but as a way to represent functional uncertainty and propagate it through multiple forward maps.

VI.4 Gravitational-wave inference and multimessenger workflows

ML also operates upstream of EoS reconstruction, in extracting source properties from gravitational-wave strain. Dingo-BNS combines physics-informed data compression, neural inference, and importance weighting for rapid binary-neutron-star parameter estimation [221]. Its scientific role is to accelerate the characterization and localization of a merger, thereby supporting timely electromagnetic follow-up and subsequent matter inference. This task is distinct from learning a common EoS across several systems: waveform parameters, individual stellar tidal responses, and a population-level EoS posterior belong to different stages of the analysis.

Importance weighting is valuable because the original likelihood can check and correct an approximate neural posterior, subject to proposal support and adequate effective sample size. It does not make a finite weighted sample an exact independent posterior ensemble. More generally, gains in inference speed should be reported alongside waveform assumptions, detector-noise robustness, and retained tidal information [221]. The same distinction matters when extending EoS learning to merger dynamics. A cold beta-equilibrated relation used for isolated stars does not alone specify the temperature, composition, and transport dependence needed for a merger calculation; this extension requires additional physical inputs rather than merely a larger network [220].

VII AI for Lattice QFT: From Reconstruction to Discovery

Lattice QFT provides the first-principles non-perturbative framework that anchors much of QCD phenomenology. It determines thermodynamic properties at vanishing or small baryon chemical potential, supplies hadronic and transport inputs, and provides benchmarks for continuum and effective descriptions. Its computational challenges are equally well known: large configuration ensembles are expensive to generate, autocorrelation times can grow near criticality and in topological sectors, real-time observables require analytic continuation from Euclidean data, and finite-density QCD suffers from the sign problem. Machine learning has therefore entered lattice QFT through several complementary routes, ranging from inverse reconstruction of physical information and recognition of phases and correlations to generative sampling and sign-problem mitigation. More recently, the scope is expanding further: rather than using AI only to accelerate a calculation within a prescribed theory, emerging approaches seek to infer the underlying operators, Hamiltonians, and effective field theories directly from data. This progression—from reconstruction and learning, through generation, toward theory discovery—provides a useful organizing principle for AI applications in lattice QFT.

VII.1 Inverse reconstruction from Euclidean data

Many lattice observables are computed in Euclidean time, whereas heavy-ion and hadron-structure applications often require real-time or spectral information. Spectral-function reconstruction from Euclidean correlators is therefore a central inverse problem. Automatic-differentiation approaches represent the spectral function by trainable parameters and optimize it through the integral relation to the Euclidean correlator [222]. Related analyses clarified how neural priors, regularization, and correlator uncertainty affect the reconstruction [223]. Similar inverse-learning methods have been applied to the heavy-quark potential in the QGP, where lattice bottomonium information is used to infer in-medium potential components [224], also applied to extract the valence parton distribution function (PDF) of pion employing next-to-next-leading-order (NNLO) perturbative QCD matching to lattice calculations for leading-twist expansion for renormalization group invariant (RGI) ratios of bilocal pion matrix elements with NNLO Wilson coefficients [225].

The significance of these studies is that ML provides flexible parameterizations and optimization tools for an ill-posed inverse problem rather than removing the ill-posedness of analytic continuation. Positivity, smoothness, asymptotic behavior, sum rules, and correlator uncertainty in the correlator must still be treated explicitly and specified. When these ingredients are included, neural reconstruction can complement maximum-entropy, Bayesian, and kernel-based methods; when they are absent, a network can easily return a plausible but non-unique answer.

VII.2 Learning phases, fields, and correlations

Before the recent rise of generative AI applications in lattice QFT, ML was already used to identify phases and order parameters in lattice and statistical field theories. Regressive and generative neural networks were applied to scalar field theory in Ref. [226], and deep-learning stochastic processes were explored in connection with QCD phase-transition dynamics [227]. These controlled systems remain valuable benchmarks because one can test whether a model learns genuine field correlations rather than artifacts of a small dataset.

For gauge theories, symmetry is the central constraint. A generic neural network does not automatically respect gauge covariance or gauge invariance. Gauge-equivariant convolutional networks [228] and equivariant flow-based samplers [229] address this by building the symmetry into the architecture. This is more reliable than relying only on data augmentation. The same lesson applies to topological sectors, chiral symmetry, and continuum extrapolation: a lattice ML method is useful only if it respects or controls the structures that make lattice QCD predictive.

VII.3 Generative models for lattice QFT, and sign-problems

Generative modeling is now one of the most active ML directions in lattice QFT studies, which is one important branch of HENP. Flow-based models were proposed as independent samplers for lattice field theory [230] and then extended to gauge theories [229]. Recent work has studied correlated lattice-QCD ensembles generated by flow models [231], stochastic normalizing flows combine non-equilibrium Monte Carlo evolution with gauge-equivariant layers and have been implemented in 4-dimensional SU(3) gauge theory [232]. Related work on SU(3) topology sampling uses open boundary conditions to reduce topological-charge autocorrelations and remove the boundary effects through a non-equilibrium switch back to periodic boundaries; a customized stochastic normalizing flow improves this strategy [233].Super-resolving normalizing flows pursue a related practical goal by mapping between lattice resolutions [234]. These efforts aim to reduce sampling cost and autocorrelation while preserving the exact target distribution or allowing controlled reweighting.

Diffusion models provide a complementary route. Ref. [236] established a direct connection between diffusion models and stochastic quantization and demonstrated diffusion-based global sampling in two-dimensional scalar lattice field theory. The reverse diffusion process can be interpreted as a learned stochastic evolution from a simple prior toward the interacting field distribution. Follow-up work analyzed how diffusion models learn higher-order cumulants [237], and related studies combined complex Langevin dynamics with score-based and energy-based diffusion models in complex-weight systems [238]. These developments are particularly relevant for finite-density and real-time problems, where the sampled distribution may be complex or difficult to represent by conventional probability densities.

Gauge theory adds further constraints. Physics-conditioned diffusion models for lattice gauge theory then try to make the coupling or action parameters explicitly in the generator [239] though not completely work well as shown in 2D U(1) case on topological sector yet. This would be important for parameter scans if the generalization or condition is achieved for different physical parameters: a single model can interpolate across ensembles only if observables, autocorrelations, and topological quantities remain correct.

Recent stochastic-path approaches push the same idea of stochastic generation toward learned Markov-chain dynamics. The Stochastic Path Sampler (SPS) constructs trainable forward and backward stochastic kernels and uses a trajectory-balance-type objective to learn nonlocal paths through configuration space [240]. From the lattice perspective, the attraction is clear: a path model can propose updates that are less local than standard molecular-dynamics or heat-bath steps. The caution is equally clear. Unless the learned sampler is embedded in an exact accept/reject correction, unbiased reweighting, or a demonstrably controlled estimator, it is a proposal mechanism rather than a replacement for lattice sampling. SPS and related trajectory-balance ideas are therefore best read as part of a broader search for trainable proposal dynamics that reduce autocorrelation while preserving the target path-integral measure. For gauge theories, SPS-like methods must still prove gauge compatibility, topology sampling, acceptance behavior, autocorrelation reduction, and continuum scaling.

Physics-informed kernels (PIKs) introduce a particularly direct connection between a specified action and generative transport in the context of lattice QFT sampling. Ref.[241] formulates the transformation through prescribed intermediate actions and kernels that can be solved and refined independently at different layers. The construction builds on physics-informed renormalization group flows, which treat the effective description and the evolving field coordinates jointly. “kernel” denotes the field-transformation generator, not a Gaussian-process covariance kernel. PIKs belong to a broader history of action-based transport, including trivializing maps and continuity-equation learning between Boltzmann distributions.

For sign problems, generative and variational methods can alter the integration manifold, learn phase-quenched corrections, or construct better proposal distributions. Neural path optimization and learned sign-fluctuation subtraction are promising, but they must be coupled to rigorous estimators and controlled benchmarks [242, 243, 244]. The complex extension of PIKs constructs transformations that preserve the integration weight while deforming the contour [245], where the reported demonstrations include zero-dimensional complex-weight theories and the real-time quantum harmonic oscillator. They provide a concrete bridge between transport equations and sign-problem mitigation A useful principle is to separate three notions: faster sampling of a positive distribution, variance reduction for a complex estimator, and unbiased recovery of the target observable. Only the last one is a complete solution.

Despite these advances, ML samplers must pass stringent lattice-QFT tests before they can be used in precision QCD. Exactness requires an accept/reject correction, unbiased reweighting, or a controlled demonstration that residual bias is negligible. Autocorrelation reduction must be measured for physical observables, not only for visual similarity of configurations. In gauge theory, topological tunneling, continuum scaling, finite-volume behavior, and chiral properties are decisive benchmarks. The field is therefore moving from proof-of-principle demonstrations toward validation standards that resemble conventional lattice methodology.

ML for lattice QFT is best understood as a set of physics-constrained numerical tools. It can help reconstruct real-time information, learn field distributions, accelerate sampling, and explore sign-problem strategies. Its long-term impact will depend on whether these tools can be combined with the rigor that makes lattice QCD first-principles: controlled systematics, continuum extrapolation, symmetry preservation, and reproducible error estimates.

VII.4 Learning Quantum Field Theories Across Scales

The developments discussed above mainly use AI to reconstruct physical observables, identify phases and correlations, or improve the sampling of a theory whose microscopic formulation is already known. A more ambitious direction is to reverse this logic: can machine learning infer the effective theory itself from physical data? This question connects AI-based inverse problems with Hamiltonian learning, effective field theory, and the renormalization group. In this setting, the objective is not merely to predict an observable, but to identify the relevant operators, their couplings, and their scale dependence, D⟶{Oi,gi}⟶Heff,D\longrightarrow\{O_{i},g_{i}\}\longrightarrow H_{\rm eff}, where DD denotes measured or simulated data, OiO_{i} are candidate operators, and gig_{i} are the corresponding effective couplings.

A particularly relevant demonstration was provided by Hamiltonian learning in quantum field theories using tunnel-coupled quantum gases [246]. As illustrated in Fig. 19, experimental measurements at finite spatial resolution are first converted into field correlation functions. These correlations are then used to determine the operator content and coupling constants of an effective QFT Hamiltonian. In the demonstrated system, the learning procedure distinguishes an interacting sine-Gordon description from a free quadratic theory and extracts the corresponding effective parameters. This example is conceptually important because the machine-learning task is no longer restricted to reconstructing a particular observable: the data are used to infer the dynamical theory that best describes the observed correlations.

The role of the resolution scale provides a natural connection to the renormalization group. In the Wilsonian picture, changing the resolution changes the effective degrees of freedom and the values of the corresponding couplings [247]. Hamiltonian learning offers a data-driven realization of this idea: rather than assuming the renormalization-group trajectory in advance, one can infer effective Hamiltonians at different resolution scales,

Heff​(Λ1)→Heff​(Λ2)→Heff​(Λ3)→⋯.H_{\rm eff}(\Lambda_{1})\;\rightarrow\;H_{\rm eff}(\Lambda_{2})\;\rightarrow\;H_{\rm eff}(\Lambda_{3})\;\rightarrow\;\cdots.

The resulting flow, {gi​(Λ)},\{g_{i}(\Lambda)\}, can in principle reveal which operators become relevant, irrelevant, or approximately scale invariant over a given range. This establishes a conceptual bridge between machine learning, Hamiltonian identification, and the emergence of effective descriptions across scales.

For lattice QFT, this perspective suggests a broader research program. Instead of using AI only to accelerate simulations within a prescribed lattice action, one could seek to learn the effective operator basis and its scale dependence directly from ensembles of lattice configurations or from combined lattice and experimental data. A physics-informed implementation would need to incorporate gauge invariance, locality, global symmetries, conservation laws, and the appropriate continuum limit. Schematically,

Dlattice→{Oi,gi​(a)}→Heff​(a)→continuum​EFT.D_{\rm lattice}\rightarrow\{O_{i},g_{i}(a)\}\rightarrow H_{\rm eff}(a)\rightarrow{\rm continuum\ EFT}.

Such an approach could complement conventional lattice calculations by providing a systematic route from microscopic lattice dynamics to coarse-grained effective descriptions.

The main challenge is that theory discovery is substantially more demanding than parameter estimation. Different operator bases can describe the same finite-resolution data, and learned Hamiltonians can suffer from non-identifiability, finite-volume effects, discretization artifacts, and statistical uncertainties. Consequently, a learned effective theory must be tested not only by its fit to the training observables, but also by its symmetry properties, predictive power for independent observables, stability under changes of resolution, and consistency with known continuum limits. These requirements are particularly important if AI-generated Hamiltonians are to be interpreted as physical theories rather than merely as flexible data representations.

Hamiltonian learning therefore represents a possible transition from AI-assisted computation to AI-assisted theory discovery. In the longer term, combining Hamiltonian learning with lattice QFT, effective field theory, renormalization-group methods, and quantum simulation could provide a data-driven framework for discovering how effective quantum field theories emerge across scales. In this sense, the role of AI in lattice QFT may ultimately extend beyond reconstructing observables or accelerating sampling to learning the structure and flow of quantum field theories themselves.

VIII Foundation models, AI agents and Quantum machine learning

VIII.1 Foundation models for HENP

The term foundation model refers to a large model pretrained on broad data and adapted to many downstream tasks. In high-energy nuclear physics, a foundation model need not be a large language model. It might be a transformer or diffusion model pretrained on particle clouds, detector-level events, lattice configurations, hydrodynamic fields, correlators, or equation of state ensembles. The motivation is transfer: many tasks share low-level structure even when labels differ. For collider physics, foundation-model ideas are already being explored for jets and event-level representations [248, 249]. In heavy-ion physics, point-cloud diffusion models are a first step toward a foundation-style event generator because they aim to learn a broad representation of hadronic final states and support downstream generation and classification tasks [41, 250].

For high-energy nuclear physics, the most plausible foundation models are domain-specific rather than universal. A heavy-ion event model should know about particle species, momentum coordinates, centrality, collision system, and detector acceptance. A lattice model should know about gauge groups, boundary conditions, lattice geometry, and actions. A neutron-star model should know about thermodynamic constraints and stellar-structure equations. Pretraining can be useful, but physics constraints and provenance are essential. Without them, a large model may become a powerful interpolator of simulation artifacts.

VIII.2 LLM-based agents and autonomous scientific workflows

An LLM agent is an AI system that leverages a large language model as its ”brain” to autonomously accomplish tasks—not merely by generating responses, but by actively taking actions in its environment. Its key components include planning, task decomposition, reflection, chain-of-thought reasoning, execution, memory management, and the ability to utilize external tools. Collectively, these functionalities form a closed-loop cycle of reasoning, acting, and observation.

Large language model (LLM) agents have moved rapidly from proof of concept to deployed pipelines in nuclear and particle physics (2025–2026). In particle physics they organize around three complementary pillars. Simulation-native experimental design is exemplified by GRACE [251], which treats detector design as a constrained search under physical law and has autonomously optimized electromagnetic calorimeters, muon spectrometers, the DarkSide-50 dark-matter detector, and the ProtoDUNE liquid-argon TPC. Autonomous data analysis is demonstrated by LLM agents that, given only a dataset and a corpus of prior literature, reproduce electroweak, QCD, and Higgs-boson measurements on open LEP and CMS data end-to-end [252] and automate HEP analysis [253, 254]. End-to-end collider phenomenology is realized by ColliderAgent [255], which carries a model from its Lagrangian through Feynman-diagram generation, matrix-element and cross-section evaluation, and detector-level simulation to exclusion limits, without package-specific glue code. The same paradigm extends to nuclear science: the Advanced Light Source has deployed the first language-model-driven accelerator control system [256], and agent–Monte-Carlo integrations now automate input-file generation, execution, and post-processing for reactor, radiation-shielding, and medical-physics simulations.

At the Institute of High Energy Physics (IHEP), the Dr. Sai multi-agent system has been deployed at the BESIII experiment, automating full-chain physics analysis from natural language queries to end-to-end workflow execution with over 90% success rate [257]. At its core lies Xiwu, the first LLM specialized for high energy physics, which outperforms GPT-4 in domain-specific code generation and knowledge reasoning [258]. These systems represent a strategic roadmap toward ”AI+HEP” and are being generalized across multiple HEP facilities in China.

What unites these efforts is a shift toward trust established by audit rather than assertion. ColliderAgent validates itself by reproducing published results across leptoquark, axion-like-particle, and higher-dimensional-operator scenarios, while companion benchmarks and prompting-strategy studies are standardizing how such systems are evaluated [259]. Persistent limitations temper this progress: anomalous outputs are flagged but not yet investigated in closed diagnostic loops, high-fidelity Geant4 or transport-code validation remains computationally expensive, and any direct interaction with hardware—accelerators or reactors—demands rigorous uncertainty quantification, hallucination mitigation, and mandatory human-in-the-loop approval for safety-critical actions. The trajectory therefore points not toward autonomous replacement but toward human–AI collaborative laboratories, in which agents act as exploratory partners that rapidly survey vast design spaces, surface non-obvious optimizations, and preserve full reproducibility, amplifying human creativity as data volumes grow through the HL-LHC era and beyond.

A concrete agentic workflow for a heavy-ion Bayesian campaign might proceed as follows. The agent proposes a design of simulation points under human-specified priors; launches containerized simulations; checks energy conservation, multiplicity ranges, and hydrodynamic stability; trains an emulator; runs calibration diagnostics; compares posterior predictive observables to data; and produces a report listing failures and suggested next simulations. At every stage, the agent’s actions are logged and the final scientific decision remains with the researcher. A lattice version would monitor acceptance, autocorrelation, and topology; a neutron-star version would check causality, stability, and posterior coverage; a literature agent would verify arXiv identifiers and journal metadata before adding references.

Ref. [260] introduced CLVisc Agent, the first LLM agent applied to hydrodynamic studies in high-energy nuclear physics. Its meta-skill operates via a scan–compose–validate workflow: it automatically parses the CLVisc source tree, generates version-specific SKILLs, encapsulates the physical meanings of parameters such as τ0\tau_{0}, η/s\eta/s, ζ/s\zeta/s, and TfrzT_{\mathrm{frz}}, and provides observable extractors. Running on kimi-cli, it handles end-to-end parameter-scan design, GPU-accelerated evolution, ensemble comparisons, and publication-quality plots. In Pb+Pb simulations, the high-temperature branch of η/s\eta/s is found to dominate viscous suppression; in O+O collisions, comparing four O16{}^{16}\mathrm{O} structure models, the agent autonomously introduces daread_{\mathrm{area}} and β2\beta_{2} as geometric diagnostics, yielding three distinct groups. This work proves that LLMs can autonomously close the research loop from code comprehension to physical interpretation, and the framework can be extended to SMASH, URQMD, and others, offering a paradigm for automated, reproducible discovery.

Recently, LQCDMaster was proposed, it is a tool-augmented, skill-guided scientific computing agent that automatically converts natural-language lattice QCD research tasks into executable PyQUDA workflows, complete with measurement scripts, job-submission artifacts, and numerical outputs [261]. It operates through a plan-then-execute architecture, where a planner formulates a physics computation plan (subject to human review) and an executor generates the corresponding code. To ensure reliability, the system integrates expert-annotated LQCD skill libraries and a deterministic Wick-contraction tool that handles the algebraically fragile components of code generation. In benchmarks across 70 state-of-the-art LQCD tasks, LQCDMaster reproduced expert-written implementations exactly to machine precision in 63 cases, reducing implementation time from hours to minutes. It has also enabled novel computations—such as light-cone distribution amplitudes and multi-baryon spectra—that were previously unattempted, demonstrating its potential to lower barriers and accelerate discovery in fundamental physics.

VIII.3 AI for High-Energy Nuclear Physics: From Symbolic Effective Laws to Scalable Many-Body Sampling

Artificial intelligence is emerging as a transformative tool in high-energy nuclear physics, where the central challenge is to connect the fundamental theory of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) to the observable structure and dynamics of nucleons and nuclei. This subsection highlights two complementary frontiers of this effort. At one end lies AI-Newton [262], a concept-driven discovery system that autonomously induces interpretable symbolic laws from noisy data—offering a pathway toward automated construction of effective interactions, scaling laws, and phenomenological models in nuclear and QCD physics. At the other end lies the Schrödinger Generator [263], a framework for high-dimensional integration and sampling that optimizes coordinate transformations to overcome the efficiency bottlenecks of conventional Monte Carlo methods, enabling stable simulations of nuclear quantum many-body states in dimensions exceeding 600 and faithfully reproducing short-range nucleon correlations in finite nuclei. Together, these works span the arc from symbolic effective laws to scalable many-body computation, reflecting two converging roles for AI in high-energy nuclear physics: one that extracts the effective laws governing strongly interacting matter, and one that makes the simulation of complex nuclear systems tractable.

AI-Newton is a concept-driven physical law discovery system developed [262], capable of autonomously deriving fundamental physics laws from raw experimental data without supervision or prior physical knowledge. The system’s core innovation lies in its three-layer knowledge base architecture—symbols, concepts, and laws—which mimics how human physicists organize knowledge, starting from simple concepts like position and time, progressively building more complex concepts such as velocity and acceleration, and ultimately forming complete physical laws. AI-Newton integrates symbolic regression with plausible reasoning techniques, using a recommendation engine to balance exploration and exploitation, and when a discovered general law fails in new scenarios, it can add new terms through plausible reasoning to revise the law. They validated the system on 46 Newtonian mechanics experiments covering scenarios such as free fall, collisions, and oscillations, with all data generated by solving differential equations and adding Gaussian noise to simulate real experimental conditions. Experimental results show that AI-Newton successfully rediscovered core physical laws including Newton’s second law, conservation of energy, and universal gravitation, with the system averaging approximately 90 physical concepts and 50 general laws discovered. The research is considered an important step toward AI-driven autonomous scientific discovery, with the team now planning to apply the system to more challenging domains such as quantum theory.

On the other hand, integration and sampling in high dimensions are among the central challenges in modern science and technology, underpinning applications that range from quantum many-body physics to Bayesian inference and artificial intelligence. While conventional Monte Carlo methods are formally scalable, their efficiency degrades rapidly when strong correlations or sharp features are present in high-dimensional configuration space. Recently, a new framework, termed the ”Schrödinger Generator”, for integration and sampling based on the explicit optimization of coordinate transformations was proposed [263]. The method decomposes the total Jacobian into two complementary components: an adaptive map that minimizes estimator variance by learning the marginal structure in each dimension, and a normalizing-flow-based transformation that captures non-factorizable correlations in the target distribution. A final resampling step guarantees unbiased sampling even when the learned transformation is imperfect. The overall workflow of ”Schrödinger Generator” and the architecture of normalizing flow are illustrated in Fig. 21. They demonstrate stable and scalable performance for nuclear quantum many-body states in dimensions exceeding 600, faithfully reproducing short-range correlations among nucleons in finite nuclei. The framework offers a physically transparent approach to high-dimensional stochastic integration and sampling, opening new possibilities for simulations of complex quantum systems.

VIII.4 Quantum machine learning

Quantum machine learning is an active but still exploratory direction for high-energy and nuclear physics [264, 265, 266, 267]. Variational quantum circuits, quantum kernel methods, and quantum autoencoders have been studied for classification, anomaly detection, and data encoding in particle-physics settings [268, 269]. For high-energy nuclear physics, potential applications include lattice-field-theory toy models, event classification, generative modeling, and hybrid quantum-classical inference.

For an example, researchers have proposed 1P1Q, a quantum encoding scheme for high-energy physics [269]. Unlike classical compression methods, 1P1Q maps each particle’s kinematics directly onto a qubit, preserving full information for quantum algorithms. The scheme was validated on two tasks: a Quantum Autoencoder (QAE) for anomaly detection, and a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) for jet classification. The QAE outperformed classical autoencoders in distinguishing signal from QCD background jets while using far fewer parameters. The VQC achieved competitive performance with greatly reduced complexity. Real-world tests using 2016 CMS collision data confirmed the method’s robustness. Figure 22 illustrates the 1P1Q encoding for the ten hardest constituents of a top-quark jet (red) versus a QCD light-flavor jet (blue), with each particle assigned to a distinct qubit. The encoding intrinsically reflects the jet’s kinematic structure: angular coordinates and transverse momentum are mapped onto the Bloch sphere, thereby preserving geometric and energy correlations among constituents. The scaling function ff in Eq.: f→1+2​π1+e−wf\rightarrow 1+\frac{2\pi}{1+e^{-w}} serves to amplify the angular separation on the Bloch sphere. These results demonstrate that 1P1Q offers a promising path for integrating quantum machine learning into collider data analysis, potentially reducing computational overhead while maintaining high performance in experimental physics workflows.

However, in general the field remains limited by hardware noise, data-loading costs, circuit depth, and the difficulty of demonstrating a quantum advantage for realistic scientific tasks.

The quantum machine learning in high-energy nuclear physics may become important when quantum simulation and quantum computing mature for real-time dynamics, finite-density systems, or Hamiltonian field theory. In the near term, quantum machine learning benchmarks should be small, transparent, and compared against strong classical baselines. Claims of advantage should include total resource accounting, not only circuit-level performance.

VIII.5 Benchmarking and community infrastructure

The field needs benchmarks designed around physics, not only architecture comparison. We propose four benchmark families. First, lattice field theory benchmarks should include scalar ϕ4\phi^{4} theory, two-dimensional U⁡(1)U(1) gauge theory, small-volume S​U​(2)SU(2) and S​U​(3)SU(3) gauge theories, sign-problem toy models, and eventually standardized lattice-QCD ensemble tasks. Metrics should include observable bias, autocorrelation time, acceptance rate, topological tunneling, continuum-scaling relevance, and wall-clock cost.

Second, heavy-ion benchmarks should include event-level datasets from transport, hydrodynamic, and hybrid simulations with standardized observables and known hidden parameters. Data formats should support particle clouds, event images, spectra, jets, and detector-smeared outputs. Metrics should include spectra, flow, correlations, centrality dependence, rare-event coverage, calibration, and performance under generator shift.

Third, neutron-star benchmarks should include synthetic and real-data-inspired ensembles of equation of state curves, mass-radius points, tidal deformabilities, X-ray spectra, and gravitational-wave likelihood summaries. Metrics should include posterior coverage, calibration, physical constraint satisfaction, sensitivity to priors, and detection power for phase transitions or exotic degrees of freedom.

Fourth, functional, EFT, and holographic benchmarks should include differential-equation solutions, FRG or DSE toy systems, spectral reconstruction tasks, and bottom-up model-inference datasets. Metrics should include residuals of physical equations, boundary-condition satisfaction, extrapolation to new parameter regimes, and uncertainty under truncation.

Benchmarks should also include negative controls. A classifier for criticality should be tested on datasets with no critical signal but similar multiplicity and flow backgrounds. A generator for hydrodynamic events should be tested on observables deliberately withheld from training. A lattice sampler should be tested on observables sensitive to topology and long-distance modes. A neutron-star inference method should be tested on mock data generated from equation of state families absent from the training set. These negative controls are essential because many AI models succeed by learning shortcuts.

Open data standards would greatly accelerate progress. Heavy-ion event data should record generator provenance, physics parameters, random seeds where possible, detector or smearing assumptions, and observable definitions. Lattice benchmark datasets should record action, coupling, lattice size, boundary conditions, algorithm history, and autocorrelation estimates. Neutron-star datasets should distinguish prior samples, posterior samples, observational likelihood summaries, and physical filters. Without such metadata, benchmark comparisons are difficult to interpret.

IX Conclusions and outlook

AI in high-energy nuclear physics is moving from pattern recognition toward scientific workflow design. Three developments define this shift. Learned representations extract information from high-dimensional events, configurations, and observations that is difficult to isolate manually. Probabilistic ML and differentiable programming propagate uncertainties through expensive inverse problems. Generative models accelerate simulation and sampling when they respect physical constraints and are validated at the level of observables and inference.

The most important future direction is a closed QCD inference loop. On the forward side, physics-respecting generative models should produce lattice configurations, hydrodynamic events, particle clouds, correlators, or equation of state functions faster and with quantified bias. On the inverse side, simulation-based inference and Bayesian pipelines should extract posteriors for equation of state, transport coefficients, phase-structure hypotheses, and effective interactions from collider and astrophysical data. Across regimes, these posteriors should be compared and combined with lattice, continuum, EFT, perturbative, and holographic constraints. The long-term value of AI will be measured by its ability to enable such cross-regime consistency tests. The phrase “closed inference loop” should not be understood as a self-confirming autonomous system. A loop trained, calibrated, and validated on the same simulator family can amplify shared biases and converge toward an opaque interpolation of the existing model rather than a more faithful description of QCD. Other risks include overfitting to a fixed benchmark suite, repeatedly reusing theory-generated data for both training and validation, losing provenance as data products are transformed, and optimizing predictive scores while discarding mechanistic interpretability. Benchmarks are therefore necessary but not sufficient. Mitigation requires independent experimental and cross-model holdouts, negative controls, explicit model-discrepancy and out-of-distribution tests, interpretable intermediate physics quantities, immutable provenance records, and periodic confrontation with first-principles constraints and genuinely new data. Human review must remain responsible for changing priors, model classes, observables, and acceptance criteria.

Several recommendations follow. Physics constraints should be built into architectures and inference pipelines wherever possible. Gauge equivariance, conservation laws, thermodynamic stability, causality, and differentiable equations are the reason a model can be trusted outside its training set. Uncertainty quantification should be treated as part of the model rather than as a post-processing step. Community benchmarks and open datasets are essential for separating robust progress from benchmark-specific success. Foundation models and agents should be developed with strict provenance, reproducibility, and validation standards. Review articles and collaborative projects should also record negative results and failure modes, because they reveal which physics constraints are missing.

Three scientific questions should guide the next generation of work. Can AI reduce the cost of first-principles or high-fidelity calculations without compromising exactness or controlled uncertainty? This is the central question for lattice samplers, hydrodynamic emulators, and differentiable solvers. Can AI improve the information extracted from existing and future data? This is the central question for heavy-ion event-level learning, neutron-star simulation-based inference, and optimized observables for criticality or CME searches. Can AI connect sectors that were historically analyzed separately? This is the central question for unified QCD inference.

The field should also be explicit about current limits. AI cannot by itself solve the sign problem in full QCD, determine the QCD critical point, or infer neutron-star core composition without assumptions. It cannot replace careful modeling of detector response, hydrodynamic uncertainty, or nuclear-theory priors. Its value is that it can make previously intractable workflows feasible, expose hidden correlations, and force assumptions to be stated in the language of priors, likelihoods, constraints, and validation tests.

The practical motivation will grow with forthcoming data. Beam-energy-scan and fixed-target programs seek rare or subtle signatures of dense QCD matter, where high-dimensional event information and optimized observables may be decisive. Next-generation heavy-ion experiments will produce large volumes of particle-level data in complex detector environments. The Electron-Ion Collider will add complementary information on nucleon and nuclear structure, where event-level and detector-level ML will be important even though the present review focuses on QCD matter. Astrophysical data streams will also expand: additional gravitational-wave detections, X-ray radius constraints, and multimessenger observations will update dense-matter posteriors. AI methods validated now on controlled simulations should be designed to ingest these future data without changing the scientific standard of inference.

This also motivates infrastructure. A benchmark created for one paper is useful but limited; a benchmark maintained across experiments and theory groups can become a community reference. The long-term goal is an ecosystem in which new AI methods are compared on common physics tasks, with shared metrics and documented systematics.

The opportunity is substantial. New data from RHIC, the LHC, the Electron-Ion Collider, FAIR/CBM, NICA, J-PARC-HI, HIAF, neutron-star observatories, and gravitational-wave detectors will arrive in forms that are increasingly high dimensional and heterogeneous. At the same time, theoretical calculations are becoming more precise and more computationally demanding. AI can help bridge this gap when it is developed as part of the physics workflow, with QCD reasoning setting the constraints and validation standards. The most promising future is one in which AI expands the range of QCD questions that can be asked quantitatively.
